lessons.title: Functions and their allowed inputs
lessons.html:
01

Functions and their allowed inputs

Principle

A function gives one output for each allowed input. The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the outputs it actually reaches. A graph passes the vertical-line test exactly when it represents a function.

Why and when

A formula can fail because a denominator is zero, an even root has a negative radicand, or a logarithm has a nonpositive argument. For a piecewise definition, the inequality attached to each branch decides the value at a boundary.

Worked solution

For f(x)=√(x+3)/(x−2), the radicand requires x≥−3 and the denominator excludes 2. Thus the domain is [−3,2)∪(2,∞). The function is defined at −3, where f(−3)=0.

Additional worked example

Find the domain of g(x)=ln(4−x)/(x+1).

The logarithm needs 4−x>0, so x<4. Also x≠−1. The domain is (−∞,−1)∪(−1,4).

Common trap. An equality is allowed for an even root but never for a logarithm argument of zero.

lessons.title: Function families and transformations
lessons.html:
02

Function families and transformations

Principle

Linear, polynomial, rational, radical, exponential, and logarithmic functions have different characteristic shapes and restrictions. A transformation is easiest to verify by tracking a known point through the input and output changes.

Why and when

Outside changes act on outputs: a scales and possibly reflects, k shifts vertically. Inside changes act on inputs: h shifts the graph horizontally and b changes horizontal scale by 1/|b|.

Worked solution

From f(x)=x², g(x)=−2(x−3)²+1 has vertex (3,1), opens downward, and is twice as steep in output. The domain is all real numbers and the range is (−∞,1].

Additional worked example

For g(x)=√(x+4)−2, give its starting point, domain, and range.

The parent graph √x moves left 4 and down 2. Start (−4,−2); domain [−4,∞); range [−2,∞).

Common trap. An inside +4 moves the graph left, not right; test the input that makes the radicand zero.

lessons.title: Angles, unit circle, and periodic graphs
lessons.html:
03

Angles, unit circle, and periodic graphs

Principle

Radian measure links an angle to arc length. Sine and cosine are unit-circle coordinates; identities follow from the circle equation. A sine or cosine graph repeats after a full turn.

Why and when

Determine reference angle and quadrant before signs. For y=A sin(B(x−h))+k, amplitude is |A|, midline is y=k, and period is 2π/|B|. These statements use radians.

Worked solution

For y=3cos(2x)−1, amplitude is 3, period is π, and midline is y=−1. The maximum is 2 at x=0; a minimum −4 occurs at x=π/2.

Additional worked example

If sin θ=5/13 and θ is in quadrant II, find cos θ and tan θ.

cos θ=−12/13 by the unit-circle identity and quadrant sign. Thus tan θ=−5/12.

Common trap. The identity determines magnitude; the quadrant determines the sign.

lessons.title: Inverse functions and restricted branches
lessons.html:
04

Inverse functions and restricted branches

Principle

An inverse reverses input and output. It exists as a function only when each output of the original has one input. Graphically, a horizontal line must meet the original graph no more than once.

Why and when

To find an inverse, write y=f(x), solve for x, then exchange x and y. Preserve the original domain and range as the inverse range and domain. Trigonometric inverses require restricted principal branches.

Worked solution

For f(x)=2x−5, solve y=2x−5 to get x=(y+5)/2. Hence f⁻¹(x)=(x+5)/2. For x², first restrict to x≥0 if the intended inverse is √x.

Additional worked example

Find the inverse of f(x)=√(x−1), x≥1, including its domain.

y=√(x−1) gives x=y²+1. Thus f⁻¹(x)=x²+1 with domain x≥0, the range of f.

Common trap. An inverse relation can fail to be a function if the original is not one-to-one.

lessons.title: Exponential and logarithmic models
lessons.html:
05

Exponential and logarithmic models

Principle

The variable is in the exponent of an exponential function. A logarithm is its inverse and asks which exponent produced a positive input. The number e is the natural base for calculus.

Why and when

Use log laws only where each argument is positive. To solve an exponential equation, isolate the powered expression and take a logarithm; to solve a log equation, invert and check its domain.

Worked solution

Solve ln(x−1)+ln(x+1)=ln 8. The domain is x>1. Combining logs gives x²−1=8, so x=3 or −3; only x=3 is allowed.

Additional worked example

Solve e^(2x)=7 for x.

Taking natural logarithms gives 2x=ln 7, so x=(ln 7)/2.

Common trap. Do not accept an algebraic root until the original logarithm arguments are checked.

lessons.title: Why limits connect rates and area
lessons.html:
06

Why limits connect rates and area

Principle

Calculus studies what happens as a step becomes arbitrarily small. A shrinking secant interval leads to an instantaneous rate; thinner rectangles lead to exact accumulated area.

Why and when

A limit concerns nearby values, not necessarily the value at the target input. The same limiting idea supports the two major operations of calculus: differentiation and integration.

Worked solution

For f(x)=x² at x=2, a step h gives average rate [(2+h)²−4]/h=4+h. As h approaches zero, the rate approaches 4.

Additional worked example

For f(x)=x³ at x=1, simplify [f(1+h)−f(1)]/h and find its limit.

The quotient is 3+3h+h²; the limit is 3.

Common trap. Cancel h only after expanding the numerator, and do not substitute h=0 into an unsimplified 0/0 form.

lessons.title: One-sided limits and failure to agree
lessons.html:
07

One-sided limits and failure to agree

Principle

A finite two-sided limit exists only if the left and right approaches settle at the same number. A point can have a different assigned value without changing that approach.

Why and when

Trace each side separately on a graph or in a piecewise rule. Distinguish a finite limit from unbounded behavior, a jump, and persistent oscillation.

Worked solution

Let f(x)=x+2 for x<1 and f(x)=x² for x≥1. The left limit is 3, the right limit is 1, and f(1)=1. Therefore the two-sided limit does not exist.

Additional worked example

Let g(x)=x² for x≠2 and g(2)=9. Find the limit as x approaches 2 and g(2).

The limit is 4; the assigned value is 9. Changing one point does not alter the values around it.

Common trap. Substitution gives the point value only after continuity has been established.

lessons.title: Limit laws and algebraic repair
lessons.html:
08

Limit laws and algebraic repair

Principle

Limit laws permit arithmetic with finite limits. Direct substitution is valid for continuous expressions where defined. The indeterminate form 0/0 signals that more analysis is needed.

Why and when

Try substitution first. If 0/0 appears, factor, combine fractions, or rationalize. Simplify on x≠c before taking the limit; the function need not be defined at c.

Worked solution

lim as x→3 of (x²−9)/(x−3) equals lim(x+3)=6 because x²−9=(x−3)(x+3) away from 3.

Additional worked example

Find lim as x→0 of [√(1+2x)−1]/x.

Multiply by the conjugate: 2/[√(1+2x)+1], which tends to 1.

Common trap. 0/0 is neither zero nor a limit value; it is a prompt to transform the expression.

lessons.title: Continuity and guaranteed crossings
lessons.html:
09

Continuity and guaranteed crossings

Principle

Continuity requires a defined point value, an existing two-sided limit, and agreement between them. On a closed interval, continuity also guarantees every intermediate output between the endpoint outputs occurs somewhere.

Why and when

At a piecewise join, compute both side limits and the assigned value. For an existence question, the intermediate value theorem requires continuity on the whole interval.

Worked solution

Let f(x)=ax+1 for x<2 and f(x)=x² for x≥2. Matching the left limit 2a+1 with f(2)=4 gives a=3/2.

Additional worked example

Explain why x³+x−1 has a root between 0 and 1.

It is a continuous polynomial; values at 0 and 1 are −1 and 1. Since zero lies between those values, a root lies in (0,1).

Common trap. The theorem guarantees existence, not a formula for the root.

lessons.title: Precise control with epsilon and delta
lessons.html:
10

Precise control with epsilon and delta

Principle

The formal limit statement says every requested output tolerance ε>0 can be met by choosing a sufficiently small input tolerance δ>0. The puncture 0<|x−a| leaves f(a) irrelevant.

Why and when

For a linear function, bound the output error by a constant times |x−a|, then choose δ in terms of ε. For more complex functions, also restrict δ so factors stay bounded.

Worked solution

For f(x)=3x+2 at a=1, L=5 and |f(x)−5|=3|x−1|. Given any ε>0, choose δ=ε/3; then 0<|x−1|<δ gives |f(x)−5|<ε.

Additional worked example

Choose δ proving lim as x→2 of (4x−1) equals 7.

Since |(4x−1)−7|=4|x−2|, δ=ε/4 works for every ε>0.

Common trap. δ must be chosen after ε is given, and the implication must cover every allowed x near a.

lessons.title: Derivative from the tangent limit
lessons.html:
11

Derivative from the tangent limit

Principle

The derivative is the limiting slope of secant lines and the instantaneous rate of output change. The tangent line at a uses both that slope and the point (a,f(a)).

Why and when

Form the difference quotient, simplify before taking the limit, then use point-slope form. Units of f′ are output units per input unit.

Worked solution

For f(x)=x²+1, [(a+h)²+1−(a²+1)]/h=2a+h; hence f′(a)=2a. At a=2, point (2,5), the tangent is y−5=4(x−2).

Additional worked example

Find the tangent line to f(x)=x³ at x=1.

f(1)=1 and f′(1)=3, so y−1=3(x−1).

Common trap. A tangent slope alone is not a line; include the point on the original graph.

lessons.title: Derivative as a function and differentiability
lessons.html:
12

Derivative as a function and differentiability

Principle

The derivative function records tangent slope at each input where that slope exists. Its sign describes direction. Differentiability implies continuity, but a continuous corner can still lack a derivative.

Why and when

Compare one-sided slopes at corners, cusps, and vertical tangents. At a jump there can be no derivative. A graph of f′ is above the axis where f rises and below it where f falls.

Worked solution

For f(x)=|x|, the left slope at zero is −1 and the right slope is +1. The function is continuous there, but its derivative is undefined at zero.

Additional worked example

For f(x)=x³−3x, where is f increasing?

f′(x)=3x²−3>0 for x<−1 and x>1, so f rises on (−∞,−1) and (1,∞).

Common trap. A zero derivative does not itself prove a maximum or minimum; check signs.

lessons.title: Power, product, and quotient rules
lessons.html:
13

Power, product, and quotient rules

Principle

Differentiate sums term by term. A product changes through either factor; a quotient’s derivative has a denominator squared and a subtraction in the numerator.

Why and when

Mark each factor before differentiating. For quotients, preserve parentheses around both numerator products and state where the denominator is nonzero.

Worked solution

For y=(x²+1)/(x−1), y′=[2x(x−1)−(x²+1)]/(x−1)²=(x²−2x−1)/(x−1)², x≠1.

Additional worked example

Differentiate y=x²(x³+1).

y′=2x(x³+1)+3x⁴=5x⁴+2x. Expanding first to x⁵+x² gives the same result.

Common trap. The derivative of uv is not u′v′.

lessons.title: Rates, velocity, and acceleration
lessons.html:
14

Rates, velocity, and acceleration

Principle

A derivative can represent any instantaneous rate. For position, velocity is signed and speed is its magnitude; acceleration is the rate of velocity change.

Why and when

Find turning times by solving v(t)=0 and checking sign changes. Displacement is final minus initial position, whereas total distance adds the magnitudes of each directional segment.

Worked solution

For s(t)=t²−4t on [0,5], v=2t−4 changes sign at t=2. Positions are 0,−4,5. Displacement is 5; distance is 4+9=13.

Additional worked example

For s(t)=t²−2t on [0,3], find displacement and distance.

The turning time is t=1. Positions 0,−1,3 give displacement 3 and distance 1+4=5.

Common trap. The difference of endpoint positions misses a reversal of direction.

lessons.title: Trigonometric derivatives in radians
lessons.html:
15

Trigonometric derivatives in radians

Principle

The standard trigonometric derivative rules use radian measure. Combining them with the chain rule handles oscillations whose angle changes at a different rate.

Why and when

Differentiate the outer trigonometric function, keep the original argument, then multiply by the derivative of the argument. Check the negative sign for cosine.

Worked solution

For y=sin(3x²), the outer derivative is cos(3x²) and the inner rate is 6x, so y′=6x cos(3x²).

Additional worked example

Differentiate y=cos(2x−1)+tan x.

y′=−2sin(2x−1)+sec²x.

Common trap. If the angle were in degrees, these derivative formulas would need an extra conversion factor.

lessons.title: The chain rule for nested change
lessons.html:
16

The chain rule for nested change

Principle

When an output depends on an intermediate quantity, rates multiply. The outer derivative is evaluated at the inner expression, not at x alone.

Why and when

Name the inner function u=g(x). Differentiate f(u) with respect to u and u with respect to x, then multiply. For several layers, repeat from outside inward.

Worked solution

For y=(1+x²)⁵, set u=1+x². Then dy/du=5u⁴ and du/dx=2x, so y′=10x(1+x²)⁴.

Additional worked example

Differentiate y=√(1+3x²).

y′=(1/2)(1+3x²)^(−1/2)·6x=3x/√(1+3x²).

Common trap. The missing inner derivative is the most common source of a wrong chain-rule answer.

lessons.title: Derivatives of inverses
lessons.html:
17

Derivatives of inverses

Principle

An inverse reverses the mapping, so a small output change of f becomes an input change of f⁻¹. The reciprocal slope rule requires a nonzero original derivative at the matching point.

Why and when

Find the point on the original graph corresponding to the inverse input, evaluate f′ there, then take the reciprocal. For inverse trig functions, use their principal branches.

Worked solution

For y=arctan(2x), the inverse-tangent rule and chain rule give y′=2/(1+4x²). For f(x)=x³ with x>0, f⁻¹(y)=y^(1/3), whose derivative is 1/[3y^(2/3)] for y>0.

Additional worked example

If f(2)=5 and f′(2)=7, find (f⁻¹)′(5).

The inverse input 5 corresponds to original input 2, so (f⁻¹)′(5)=1/7.

Common trap. Do not use 1/f′(5); the derivative is evaluated at the matching original input f⁻¹(5).

lessons.title: Implicit differentiation
lessons.html:
18

Implicit differentiation

Principle

A curve may be defined by an equation without solving explicitly for y. Differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x, then solve for y′.

Why and when

Every derivative of a term involving y needs a chain-rule factor y′. Product terms involving x and y need the product rule. Evaluate a slope only at a point that satisfies the original relation.

Worked solution

For x²+xy+y²=7, differentiate to 2x+y+xy′+2yy′=0. Thus y′=−(2x+y)/(x+2y). At (1,2), the slope is −4/5.

Additional worked example

For x²+y²=25, find the tangent slope at (3,4).

2x+2yy′=0, so y′=−x/y=−3/4 at the given point.

Common trap. Differentiating y² as 2y omits the rate at which y changes with x.

lessons.title: Exponential and logarithmic derivatives
lessons.html:
19

Exponential and logarithmic derivatives

Principle

The natural exponential has derivative equal to itself; the natural logarithm has reciprocal derivative. A changing exponent or argument still contributes its inner derivative.

Why and when

Check the function domain first. Apply chain or product rules as needed; for ln|u| the derivative formula holds where u≠0.

Worked solution

For y=e^(2x)ln x on x>0, y′=2e^(2x)ln x+e^(2x)/x=e^(2x)(2ln x+1/x).

Additional worked example

Differentiate y=ln(x²+1).

y′=2x/(x²+1), defined for all real x.

Common trap. The reciprocal rule applies to the argument, so multiply by its derivative.

lessons.title: Related rates with changing geometry
lessons.html:
20

Related rates with changing geometry

Principle

Several quantities can change together while satisfying one geometric relation. Differentiate the relation with respect to time before inserting values from a single instant.

Why and when

Draw and label the geometry; identify given rates with signs and units; differentiate; substitute current dimensions and solve for the unknown rate.

Worked solution

A spherical balloon has V=(4/3)πr³. If r=2 cm and dr/dt=0.5 cm/s, then dV/dt=4πr² dr/dt=8π cm³/s.

Additional worked example

A circular stain has radius 3 cm and grows at 2 cm/s. How fast does its area grow?

A=πr² gives dA/dt=2πr dr/dt=12π cm²/s.

Common trap. Substituting the current radius before differentiating makes a changing variable look constant.

lessons.title: Linear approximation and differentials
lessons.html:
21

Linear approximation and differentials

Principle

Near a known input, a smooth curve is approximately its tangent line. The differential dy=f′(a)dx estimates output change and gives a fast local error or measurement estimate.

Why and when

Choose a convenient a near the requested input, compute f(a) and f′(a), then multiply by the small displacement Δx. State that the result is an approximation.

Worked solution

Estimate √9.2. With f(x)=√x at a=9, f(9)=3, f′(9)=1/6, and Δx=0.2. The estimate is 3+0.2/6≈3.0333.

Additional worked example

Estimate (8.12)^(1/3) using a=8.

f(8)=2, f′(8)=1/12, Δx=0.12, so the estimate is 2.01.

Common trap. Δx is target minus anchor, not the target input itself.

lessons.title: Absolute extrema and critical points
lessons.html:
22

Absolute extrema and critical points

Principle

A continuous function on a closed interval has an absolute maximum and minimum. The value can occur at an endpoint or at an interior point where the derivative is zero or undefined.

Why and when

Find critical inputs inside the interval, evaluate the original function there and at both endpoints, then compare actual values. A critical point is only a candidate.

Worked solution

For f(x)=x³−3x on [−2,2], f′=3(x²−1), so test −2,−1,1,2. Values are −2,2,−2,2. Maximum 2 and minimum −2 each occur twice.

Additional worked example

Find absolute extrema of f(x)=x²−4x+1 on [0,5].

Check 0,2,5: values 1,−3,6. Minimum −3 at 2; maximum 6 at 5.

Common trap. Testing only derivative zeros can miss an endpoint maximum.

lessons.title: The mean value theorem
lessons.html:
23

The mean value theorem

Principle

If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), at least one tangent slope equals the secant slope across the full interval. Equal endpoint values give Rolle’s special case: some interior tangent is horizontal.

Why and when

Check both hypotheses before solving for c. The theorem gives existence, and an algebraic derivative can locate the point in simple examples.

Worked solution

For f(x)=x² on [1,3], the secant slope is (9−1)/(3−1)=4. Since f′(x)=2x, the required c is 2.

Additional worked example

For f(x)=x³ on [0,2], find a c guaranteed by the theorem.

Secant slope is (8−0)/2=4; solve 3c²=4 to get c=2/√3 inside (0,2).

Common trap. A jump or corner invalidates a hypothesis; the conclusion cannot be invoked automatically.

lessons.title: Read the shape from derivative signs
lessons.html:
24

Read the shape from derivative signs

Principle

The first derivative reports direction; the second reports how slope changes. A sign change in f′ can classify an extremum, while a sign change in f″ marks a genuine change of concavity.

Why and when

Locate zeros and undefined points of derivatives, make a sign chart on the resulting intervals, then translate signs into a graph narrative.

Worked solution

For f(x)=x³−3x, f′=3(x−1)(x+1) changes + to − at −1 and − to + at 1. There is a local maximum at −1 and minimum at 1. Since f″=6x changes sign at 0, (0,0) is an inflection point.

Additional worked example

Does f(x)=x⁴ have an inflection point at zero?

No. f″=12x² is zero at zero but stays nonnegative on both sides. The concavity does not change.

Common trap. A zero second derivative is only a candidate for inflection, never sufficient evidence.

lessons.title: End behavior and asymptotes
lessons.html:
25

End behavior and asymptotes

Principle

A limit at infinity describes long-run behavior. For rational functions, compare highest powers: equal degrees give a coefficient ratio; a lower numerator degree gives zero; a larger numerator degree usually grows without a finite horizontal limit.

Why and when

Divide numerator and denominator by the highest relevant power. For a vertical asymptote, inspect one-sided behavior near a denominator zero not removed by cancellation.

Worked solution

As x→∞, (3x²−1)/(2x²+x) becomes (3−1/x²)/(2+1/x), so the limit is 3/2 and y=3/2 is a horizontal asymptote.

Additional worked example

Find the limit at infinity of (5x+1)/(x²+1).

The denominator has higher degree, so the limit is 0; y=0 is a horizontal asymptote.

Common trap. A cancelled denominator factor can create a hole instead of a vertical asymptote.

lessons.title: Optimization from a constraint
lessons.html:
26

Optimization from a constraint

Principle

An optimization problem needs an objective and a constraint. The constraint removes extra variables; the feasible interval tells which mathematical candidates make physical sense.

Why and when

Sketch and label, write the objective, substitute the constraint, differentiate, compare critical and boundary values, and give the requested dimensions and units.

Worked solution

A rectangle with perimeter 20 has x+y=10. Area A=x(10−x), 0≤x≤10, and A′=10−2x. Maximum occurs at x=y=5, with area 25.

Additional worked example

A 24 m fence makes three sides of a rectangle against a wall. Find the maximum area.

With widths x and length y, 2x+y=24. A=x(24−2x), so A′=24−4x=0 at x=6, y=12. Maximum area is 72 m².

Common trap. A wall replaces one fence side; using a four-sided perimeter gives the wrong model.

lessons.title: L Hospital rule after a form check
lessons.html:
27

L Hospital rule after a form check

Principle

Certain 0/0 or ∞/∞ quotients can be evaluated through a quotient of derivatives when f and g are differentiable nearby, g′ stays nonzero there, and the derivative quotient has a limit or diverges appropriately. The rule does not say the derivative of a quotient equals f′/g′.

Why and when

Substitute first to verify 0/0 or ∞/∞. If another form appears, transform it into a quotient or use an earlier technique. Recheck the form before applying the rule again.

Worked solution

lim as x→0 of (e^x−1)/x is 0/0. Differentiating numerator and denominator separately yields lim e^x/1=1.

Additional worked example

Find lim as x→0 of sin(3x)/x.

It is 0/0; derivatives give lim 3cos(3x)/1=3.

Common trap. Do not apply the rule to 1/0 or to a quotient whose numerator and denominator do not form an indeterminate pair.

lessons.title: Newton iteration for approximate roots
lessons.html:
28

Newton iteration for approximate roots

Principle

The tangent at a current guess meets the x-axis at a revised guess. Repeating can converge rapidly near a simple root, but a zero derivative or poor starting point can fail.

Why and when

Choose a plausible starting value, compute f and f′ there, update, and check the residual |f(x_n)|. Stop when the residual or successive change meets the requested tolerance.

Worked solution

For f(x)=x²−2 and x₀=1.5, f(x₀)=0.25 and f′(x₀)=3. Thus x₁=1.5−0.25/3=17/12≈1.4167, closer to √2.

Additional worked example

Use one Newton step for f(x)=x²−3, starting at x₀=2.

f(2)=1 and f′(2)=4, so x₁=2−1/4=1.75.

Common trap. A small step is not enough evidence by itself; inspect the residual as well.

lessons.title: Antiderivatives and initial conditions
lessons.html:
29

Antiderivatives and initial conditions

Principle

Antidifferentiation reverses a derivative on an interval. Every antiderivative differs by a constant. An initial condition selects one member of the family.

Why and when

Integrate each term, include C, use the initial condition, then differentiate the result to confirm the original rate.

Worked solution

If F′(x)=6x²−4 and F(1)=5, then F(x)=2x³−4x+C. Since 2−4+C=5, C=7.

Additional worked example

Find F when F′(x)=3x²+2x and F(0)=−1.

F(x)=x³+x²−1.

Common trap. The power rule for integration excludes exponent −1; that case gives ln|x|.

lessons.title: From finite sums to exact accumulation
lessons.html:
30

From finite sums to exact accumulation

Principle

A finite sum estimates accumulated quantity with rectangles of height times width. As widths shrink, the limiting sum gives the definite integral for an integrable function.

Why and when

Identify interval length, number of slices, width Δx, and sample point. Left and right sums can bracket an increasing function, but the integral is the exact limit, not either finite estimate.

Worked solution

For f(x)=x on [0,2] with two width-one slices, the left sum is 0+1=1 and the right sum is 1+2=3. The exact integral is 2.

Additional worked example

For f(x)=x² on [0,2], compute the two-rectangle left and right sums.

Width is 1. Left heights 0 and 1 give 1; right heights 1 and 4 give 5. The exact integral 8/3 lies between them.

Common trap. A rectangle estimate depends on the chosen sample point; keep the width factor.

lessons.title: The definite integral and signed area
lessons.html:
31

The definite integral and signed area

Principle

The definite integral adds contributions with sign. A portion below the x-axis subtracts from a portion above. Geometric area instead adds positive magnitudes.

Why and when

Split an interval where f changes sign if the question asks for total area or distance. Reverse bounds to reverse integral sign; joining adjacent intervals adds their integrals.

Worked solution

For f(x)=x on [−1,1], equal triangles below and above the axis cancel, giving integral 0. The geometric area is 1/2+1/2=1.

Additional worked example

Evaluate ∫ from −1 to 2 of x dx and the total geometric area.

Signed integral [x²/2] from −1 to 2 is 3/2. Areas are 1/2 below plus 2 above, totaling 5/2.

Common trap. A signed net integral can be zero even when the region has positive area.

lessons.title: The fundamental theorem in both directions
lessons.html:
32

The fundamental theorem in both directions

Principle

Accumulation changes at the current rate. Conversely, an antiderivative evaluates net accumulation between bounds. This is the bridge between derivatives and integrals.

Why and when

For a variable upper bound g(x), evaluate the integrand at g(x) and multiply by g′(x). For a definite integral, find F with F′=f and compute upper minus lower.

Worked solution

For A(x)=∫₀^(x²) cos t dt, A′(x)=2x cos(x²). Also ∫₀²3x² dx=[x³]₀²=8.

Additional worked example

Differentiate ∫₁^(3x) √(1+t²) dt.

The derivative is 3√(1+9x²).

Common trap. A changing upper bound contributes its own derivative; omitting it loses the chain-rule factor.

lessons.title: Net change and basic integral rules
lessons.html:
33

Net change and basic integral rules

Principle

Accumulating a rate gives net change in the underlying quantity. Integrals of sums can be separated, and symmetry can shorten work on a centered interval.

Why and when

Identify the rate and its units. Integrate it over time for displacement or net production. For total distance or gross amount, account for sign changes instead of using net change alone.

Worked solution

If velocity is v(t)=2t−4 on [0,5], displacement is ∫₀⁵v dt=[t²−4t]₀⁵=5. The velocity changes sign at t=2; distance is 4+9=13.

Additional worked example

A tank receives water at r(t)=3t² liters/minute over 0≤t≤2. How much enters?

∫₀²3t² dt=[t³]₀²=8 liters.

Common trap. The units of an integrated rate are the original quantity, not quantity per time.

lessons.title: Substitution reverses the chain rule
lessons.html:
34

Substitution reverses the chain rule

Principle

A nested integrand becomes simpler when the inner expression is renamed and its derivative supplies the differential. For definite integrals, transform the bounds as well.

Why and when

Choose u, compute du, rewrite the entire integrand in u, change bounds if present, integrate, and either return to x or evaluate in u. Verify by differentiation.

Worked solution

∫₀¹2x(1+x²)³ dx: set u=1+x², du=2x dx. Bounds 0→1 and 1→2 yield ∫₁²u³ du=[u⁴/4]₁²=15/4.

Additional worked example

Evaluate ∫₀¹6x/(1+3x²) dx.

u=1+3x², du=6x dx; new bounds 1 and 4. Integral ∫₁⁴du/u=ln 4.

Common trap. Changing the integrand but retaining the old x-bounds mixes two variables.

lessons.title: Exponential and logarithmic antiderivatives
lessons.html:
35

Exponential and logarithmic antiderivatives

Principle

These patterns reverse the chain rule. A base e exponential integrates to itself after accounting for the inner rate; a reciprocal inner-rate pattern integrates to a logarithm.

Why and when

Look for the derivative of the exponent or denominator, adjusting a constant factor if necessary. Use ln|u| where u can be positive or negative on a valid interval.

Worked solution

∫[e^(2x)+3/x] dx=(1/2)e^(2x)+3ln|x|+C, on intervals avoiding zero.

Additional worked example

Evaluate ∫₀¹2e^(2x) dx.

An antiderivative is e^(2x); the result is e²−1.

Common trap. The factor 1/2 is needed in ∫e^(2x)dx because differentiating e^(2x) produces 2e^(2x).

lessons.title: Inverse trigonometric integral patterns
lessons.html:
36

Inverse trigonometric integral patterns

Principle

The derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions produce recognizable rational and radical integrands. The arcsine pattern requires |u|<1 for the derivative formula.

Why and when

First normalize any constant a and look for an inner substitution. Differentiate the proposed inverse function to confirm the coefficient and domain.

Worked solution

∫₀¹ 1/(1+x²) dx=[arctan x]₀¹=π/4. The denominator’s plus sign identifies inverse tangent.

Additional worked example

Find ∫ 2/(1+4x²) dx.

Let u=2x, du=2dx; the result is arctan(2x)+C.

Common trap. A 1−u² radical suggests arcsine; a 1+u² denominator suggests arctangent.

lessons.title: Area between two curves
lessons.html:
37

Area between two curves

Principle

A vertical slice has height equal to upper curve minus lower curve. Summing these heights across the interval gives area. Crossings require new upper-lower decisions.

Why and when

Find intersections, test which curve is higher on each interval, split where that ordering changes, and integrate a nonnegative height.

Worked solution

Between y=x and y=x² for 0≤x≤1, x≥x², so area is ∫₀¹(x−x²)dx=[x²/2−x³/3]₀¹=1/6.

Additional worked example

Find the enclosed area between y=2x and y=x².

They meet at x=0 and x=2. Area ∫₀²(2x−x²)dx=4/3.

Common trap. An unsigned area cannot be a negative result; recheck the curve order.

lessons.title: Volumes by slicing disks and washers
lessons.html:
38

Volumes by slicing disks and washers

Principle

A solid can be built from thin cross sections. Rotation about an axis gives disks when there is no hole and washers when an inner boundary leaves a hole. The radii are distances to the axis.

Why and when

Draw one representative slice perpendicular to the rotation axis, identify outer radius R and inner radius r, square each separately, then integrate.

Worked solution

Rotate the region between y=2 and y=x on [0,2] about the x-axis. Outer radius is 2 and inner radius is x, so V=π∫₀²(4−x²)dx=16π/3.

Additional worked example

Rotate the region under y=x, 0≤x≤2, about the x-axis. Find the volume.

The inner radius is zero. V=π∫₀²x² dx=8π/3 cubic units.

Common trap. A washer area is π(R²−r²), not π(R−r)².

lessons.title: Cylindrical shells and method choice
lessons.html:
39

Cylindrical shells and method choice

Principle

A slice parallel to the axis of rotation forms a thin cylindrical shell. Its volume is circumference times height times thickness. Shells can avoid solving a curve for the other coordinate.

Why and when

Draw a representative strip. Radius is its distance to the axis; height is the region’s upper-lower span. Integrate over strip positions. Compare with disks or washers by which gives the simpler setup.

Worked solution

Rotate the region under y=x, 0≤x≤2, about the y-axis. A vertical strip has radius x and height x, so V=2π∫₀²x² dx=16π/3.

Additional worked example

Rotate the region under y=x², 0≤x≤1, about the y-axis. Use shells.

Radius x, height x²: V=2π∫₀¹x³ dx=π/2.

Common trap. A shell uses radius times height; squaring the height would produce a different volume.

lessons.title: Functions, domains, and piecewise rules
lessons.html:
01

Functions, domains, and piecewise rules

Idea

A function assigns exactly one output to every allowed input. Domain is the allowed input set; range is the outputs actually produced. A piecewise rule first asks which condition the input satisfies, then applies only that branch.

First move

For a formula, exclude zero denominators and negative radicands under even roots. For a piecewise graph, inspect the endpoint condition before evaluating. An open circle excludes its point; a filled circle includes it.

Worked reasoning

Let f(x)=√(x+2)/(x−1). The square root needs x≥−2 and the denominator needs x≠1, so the domain is [−2,1)∪(1,∞). For g(x)=x+1 when x<0 and x² when x≥0, g(0)=0, while the left-hand values approach 1.

Additional worked example

Find the domain of h(x)=√(5−x)/(x+2). Then give h(5).

The domain is (−∞,−2)∪(−2,5]. The endpoint 5 is allowed and h(5)=0. Exclude −2 even though the radicand is valid there.

If it went wrong. If you wrote x<5, you excluded a valid square-root endpoint. If you included −2, you overlooked the denominator.

Optional visual explanationNick Kaneko · Relations and Functions ↗

lessons.title: Transformation, combination, and composition
lessons.html:
02

Transformation, combination, and composition

Idea

Outside changes affect outputs; inside changes affect inputs. Addition and multiplication combine outputs at the same x. Composition sends the output of one function into the input of another, so its domain must satisfy both rules.

First move

To evaluate f(g(x)), compute g first, then apply f. For a graph transformation, test one landmark point rather than memorizing a sign slogan.

Worked reasoning

If f(x)=√x and g(x)=x−3, then (f∘g)(x)=√(x−3), whose domain is x≥3. In contrast, (g∘f)(x)=√x−3, whose domain is x≥0. The two compositions have different graphs and domains.

Additional worked example

For f(x)=1/x and g(x)=x+2, find (f∘g)(x) and its domain.

(f∘g)(x)=1/(x+2), with x≠−2. The restriction comes from the input reaching zero inside f.

If it went wrong. If you excluded x=0 instead, you checked f’s original input before composition rather than the actual input g(x).

Optional visual explanationNick Kaneko · Intro to Transformations ↗

lessons.title: Exponent rules before exponential models
lessons.html:
03

Exponent rules before exponential models

Idea

Exponent rules operate on powers with the same nonzero base. A negative exponent is a reciprocal, and a fractional exponent is a root where the real-valued root exists. An exponential function keeps the base fixed and lets the exponent vary.

First move

Rewrite negative and fractional powers before simplifying. Match bases before combining exponents; addition of powered terms does not follow a product rule.

Worked reasoning

For x>0, x^(3/2)·x^(−1/2)=x^(1)=x. But x²+x³ cannot be replaced by x⁵; factoring gives x²(1+x). For 2^(x+1)=16, write 16=2⁴ and solve x+1=4, so x=3.

Additional worked example

Simplify (x³/x^(−2))^(1/5) for x>0.

Inside, x³/x^(−2)=x⁵. The fifth root gives x. The condition x>0 makes every fractional-power step unambiguous here.

If it went wrong. Subtracting exponents means 3−(−2)=5; subtracting 2 instead reverses the denominator’s negative sign.

lessons.title: Exponentials and logarithms as inverses
lessons.html:
04

Exponentials and logarithms as inverses

Idea

A logarithm asks which exponent produces a positive number. Products become sums of logarithms; powers become coefficients. A logarithm never accepts zero or a negative argument.

First move

Condense or expand only when all logarithm arguments are positive. When solving, isolate the logarithm or exponential, invert it, and check the original domain.

Worked reasoning

Solve ln(x−1)+ln(x+1)=ln 8. The domain requires x>1. Then ln(x²−1)=ln 8, so x²−1=8, giving x=3 or −3. Only x=3 survives the domain check.

Additional worked example

Solve 2 ln x=ln 9.

x>0 and ln(x²)=ln 9 imply x²=9; therefore x=3, not ±3.

If it went wrong. The logarithm domain removes the negative algebraic root; do not accept roots before checking the original equation.

Optional visual explanationCallie Rethman · Exponential Functions ↗

lessons.title: Trigonometric models and inverse values
lessons.html:
05

Trigonometric models and inverse values

Idea

Radians connect angle to arc length and make calculus derivative formulas work without extra factors. Sine and cosine describe coordinates on the unit circle. Inverse trigonometric functions return a principal angle, not every angle with that value.

First move

Locate quadrant and reference angle before assigning signs. For an identity, replace one expression with an equivalent one on its valid domain; never cancel through a possible zero denominator.

Worked reasoning

If sin θ=3/5 and θ lies in quadrant II, then cos θ=−4/5 and tan θ=−3/4. The magnitude follows from the Pythagorean identity; quadrant II fixes the sign.

Additional worked example

Evaluate arcsin(−1/2), using its principal range.

−π/6, since arcsin returns an angle in [−π/2,π/2].

If it went wrong. A coterminal or quadrant-III angle may have the same sine but is outside arcsin’s output range.

lessons.title: Amplitude, period, and graph shifts
lessons.html:
06

Amplitude, period, and graph shifts

Idea

Amplitude measures vertical distance from the midline to a peak; period measures the horizontal length of one cycle. The midline is y=k. A phase shift moves landmarks horizontally, while a negative A reflects the sine wave about its midline.

First move

Read A, B, h, and k from a parenthesized argument. Mark one cycle using quarter-period steps; then apply the vertical scale and midline.

Worked reasoning

For y=2sin(3x)+1, amplitude is 2, midline is y=1, and period is 2π/3. Starting at x=0, one cycle reaches a maximum 3 at x=π/6 and a minimum −1 at x=π/2.

Additional worked example

For y=−3cos(2(x−π/4))+2, state amplitude, period, midline, and value at x=π/4.

Amplitude 3, period π, midline y=2, and y(π/4)=−3cos(0)+2=−1.

If it went wrong. The phase shift is π/4, not π/2: the argument already has the form 2(x−h).

lessons.title: Approach from both sides
lessons.html:
07

Approach from both sides

Idea

A limit is the value approached near c; it can differ from f(c). A two-sided finite limit exists only if both one-sided approaches agree. A hole changes the function value but need not change the limit.

First move

From a graph or piecewise rule, trace toward c from the left and right separately. State a two-sided limit only after comparing them.

Worked reasoning

Let f(x)=x+1 for x<2, and f(x)=x² for x≥2. The left limit at 2 is 3, the right limit is 4, and f(2)=4. Because 3≠4, the two-sided limit does not exist.

Additional worked example

Let g(x)=x² for x≠1 and g(1)=7. Find the limit as x approaches 1 and g(1).

The limit is 1, while g(1)=7. The isolated assigned value does not control nearby behavior.

If it went wrong. Substituting the point value for the limit confuses the output at c with the approach to c.

Optional visual explanationCallie Rethman · One-Sided Limits ↗

lessons.title: Algebraic limits and continuity
lessons.html:
08

Algebraic limits and continuity

Idea

Direct substitution works when the expression is continuous at the point. An apparent 0/0 is a signal to simplify, not an answer. Continuity requires an existing limit, a defined point value, and equality between them.

First move

Substitute first. If 0/0 appears, factor, rationalize, or simplify on a punctured neighborhood. For a piecewise join, match the two side limits and the assigned value.

Worked reasoning

lim as x→3 of (x²−9)/(x−3) is not 0/0. For x≠3, factor to x+3; its limit is 6. Defining the missing value as 6 would make the function continuous at 3.

Additional worked example

Choose a so f(x)=ax+1 for x<2 and f(x)=x² for x≥2 is continuous at 2.

The right limit and point value are 4. Match 2a+1=4, so a=3/2.

If it went wrong. Matching only branch formulas is insufficient if the branch with equality assigns a different point value.

lessons.title: From secant to tangent
lessons.html:
09

From secant to tangent

Idea

A derivative is the limit of average change over a shrinking interval. It is the tangent slope and the instantaneous rate, with output units divided by input units.

First move

When a problem asks for instantaneous slope or rate, compute f′ at the given input. A tangent line also needs the point (c,f(c)).

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x², [f(c+h)−f(c)]/h=[(c+h)²−c²]/h=2c+h, so f′(c)=2c. At c=3, the tangent through (3,9) has slope 6: y−9=6(x−3).

Additional worked example

Find the tangent line to f(x)=x²+1 at x=2.

f(2)=5 and f′(2)=4, so y−5=4(x−2).

If it went wrong. A tangent slope alone is not the tangent line; include the function’s point value.

Optional visual explanationNick Kaneko · Slopes of Tangent Lines ↗

lessons.title: Read derivative graphs and corners
lessons.html:
10

Read derivative graphs and corners

Idea

The sign of f′ reports increasing or decreasing behavior. A zero derivative gives a horizontal tangent but does not by itself prove an extremum. A corner or jump can prevent differentiability.

First move

Read the slope of f to infer f′, and check one-sided slopes at a corner. Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity alone does not imply differentiability.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=|x|, the left slope at 0 is −1 and the right slope is +1. The function is continuous at 0, but f′(0) does not exist. For x³, f′(0)=0 yet there is no local extremum.

Additional worked example

For f(x)=x³−3x, identify intervals where f rises.

f′(x)=3x²−3=3(x−1)(x+1), positive on (−∞,−1) and (1,∞).

If it went wrong. A critical point is a candidate; classify it by sign change or another valid test.

lessons.title: Basic and higher derivatives
lessons.html:
11

Basic and higher derivatives

Idea

Differentiate a sum term by term. The second derivative measures how the first derivative changes and later helps classify concavity and acceleration.

First move

Simplify a polynomial first, apply the power rule to each term, and keep the original variable. Differentiate again only when the question asks for acceleration, concavity, or higher-order change.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=4x³−5x+7, f′(x)=12x²−5 and f″(x)=24x. At x=2 the slope is 43 and the second derivative is 48.

Additional worked example

Find the velocity and acceleration when s(t)=t³−6t²+2t.

v(t)=3t²−12t+2; a(t)=6t−12. Position, velocity, and acceleration have successive time derivatives.

If it went wrong. The derivative of a constant is zero; do not leave the +7 or its analogue in a derivative.

lessons.title: Products, quotients, and nested functions
lessons.html:
12

Products, quotients, and nested functions

Idea

A product has two changing factors, so both contribute. A nested function has an inner rate, which multiplies the outer rate. A quotient has a denominator squared.

First move

Mark the factors and inner expression before differentiating. Do not apply the power rule to an entire product unless it has first been algebraically expanded.

Worked reasoning

For y=x²(3x+1)⁴, treat x² and (3x+1)⁴ as factors. Then y′=2x(3x+1)⁴+12x²(3x+1)³. The 12 comes from 4 times the inner derivative 3.

Additional worked example

Differentiate y=(x²+1)/(x−1).

y′=[2x(x−1)−(x²+1)]/(x−1)²=(x²−2x−1)/(x−1)², for x≠1.

If it went wrong. If your quotient numerator has a plus sign between the two products, recheck the quotient rule.

Optional visual explanationCallie Rethman · Intro to the Chain Rule ↗

lessons.title: Trigonometric derivatives
lessons.html:
13

Trigonometric derivatives

Idea

These rules assume radians. When a trigonometric expression contains an inner function, multiply by its derivative.

First move

Identify the outer trig function and its argument. Differentiate the argument last. Check signs, especially for cosine.

Worked reasoning

For y=sin(3x²), the outer derivative is cos(3x²) and the inner derivative is 6x, so y′=6x cos(3x²).

Additional worked example

Differentiate y=cos(2x−1)+tan x.

y′=−2 sin(2x−1)+sec²x.

If it went wrong. The factor 2 is required by the chain rule; cosine also supplies a minus sign.

lessons.title: Motion, velocity, and acceleration
lessons.html:
14

Motion, velocity, and acceleration

Idea

Velocity has direction; speed is its magnitude. A particle moves right when velocity is positive and left when negative. Acceleration is change in velocity, not necessarily change in speed.

First move

Differentiate position, find where velocity changes sign, and interpret intervals. Total distance adds absolute changes in position; displacement is final minus initial position.

Worked reasoning

For s(t)=t²−4t on 0≤t≤5, v=2t−4 changes sign at t=2. Positions are s(0)=0, s(2)=−4, s(5)=5. Displacement is 5; total distance is 4+9=13.

Additional worked example

For s(t)=t²−2t on 0≤t≤3, find displacement and total distance.

Positions at t=0,1,3 are 0,−1,3. Displacement is 3 and total distance is 1+4=5.

If it went wrong. Using s(3)−s(0) for distance misses the reversal at t=1.

lessons.title: Implicit relations and related rates
lessons.html:
15

Implicit relations and related rates

Idea

When x and y are linked, differentiate every occurrence of y with the chain rule. For changing geometry, differentiate with respect to time before inserting a snapshot of the dimensions.

First move

Write a relation, label known rates with signs and units, differentiate, then substitute the instant’s values.

Worked reasoning

If x²+y²=25, then 2x+2yy′=0, so y′=−x/y where y≠0. For a circle A=πr², dA/dt=2πr dr/dt; at r=3 cm and dr/dt=2 cm/s, dA/dt=12π cm²/s.

Additional worked example

A sphere has V=(4/3)πr³. At r=2 cm and dr/dt=0.5 cm/s, how fast does volume change?

dV/dt=4πr² dr/dt=4π(4)(0.5)=8π cm³/s.

If it went wrong. Substituting r=2 before differentiating would turn a changing radius into a constant.

Optional visual explanationNick Kaneko · Intro to Related Rates ↗

lessons.title: Linear estimates and differentials
lessons.html:
16

Linear estimates and differentials

Idea

Near a known input, the tangent line provides a local estimate. The differential dy=f′(x)dx estimates output change, with error usually growing as the step grows.

First move

Choose a convenient anchor a close to the target, calculate f(a) and f′(a), then multiply the derivative by the small input change.

Worked reasoning

Estimate √(4.1) using f(x)=√x at a=4. Since f(4)=2, f′(4)=1/4, and Δx=0.1, the estimate is 2+0.025=2.025.

Additional worked example

Estimate (8.12)^(1/3) using a=8.

f(8)=2, f′(8)=1/(3·8^(2/3))=1/12, Δx=0.12, so the estimate is 2.01.

If it went wrong. Use the derivative at the anchor and the difference from that anchor, not the target itself as Δx.

lessons.title: Candidates for absolute extrema
lessons.html:
17

Candidates for absolute extrema

Idea

On a closed interval, a continuous function reaches a largest and a smallest value. A critical point is where the derivative is zero or undefined; it is a candidate, not automatically an extremum.

First move

Differentiate, find interior critical points, evaluate the original function at each candidate and both endpoints, then compare values.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x³−3x on [−2,2], f′=3(x²−1), so check x=−2,−1,1,2. Their values are −2,2,−2,2. The absolute maximum is 2 and minimum is −2, each attained twice.

Additional worked example

Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x)=x²−4x+1 on [0,5].

f′=2x−4 vanishes at 2. Values f(0)=1, f(2)=−3, f(5)=6. Minimum −3 at 2; maximum 6 at 5.

If it went wrong. If you selected only x=2, you skipped endpoints, one of which gives the maximum.

lessons.title: Increasing, decreasing, and concavity
lessons.html:
18

Increasing, decreasing, and concavity

Idea

The first derivative controls direction; the second derivative controls how slope changes. A sign change in f′ can classify a local extremum. A sign change in f″ can identify an inflection point, provided the function is continuous there.

First move

Use sign intervals rather than isolated derivative values. Mark places where f′ or f″ is zero or undefined, test intervals, and verify that the claimed point belongs to the graph.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x³−3x, f′=3(x²−1): rise, fall, rise across −1 and 1. Thus a local maximum occurs at −1 and a local minimum at 1. Since f″=6x changes sign at 0, the graph has an inflection point at (0,0).

Additional worked example

For f(x)=x⁴, classify x=0 using f′ and f″.

f′=4x³ changes from negative to positive at 0, so 0 is a local minimum. f″=12x² is zero at 0 but stays nonnegative, so 0 is not an inflection point.

If it went wrong. A zero second derivative is only a candidate; without a concavity sign change there is no inflection.

lessons.title: Build and test an optimization model
lessons.html:
19

Build and test an optimization model

Idea

An applied maximum or minimum needs a quantity to optimize and a constraint that removes extra variables. The feasible domain is part of the solution, and the final answer must use the asked-for units.

First move

Draw and label the situation, write the objective, use the constraint to reduce it to one variable, differentiate, compare candidate and boundary values, then interpret.

Worked reasoning

A rectangle with perimeter 20 has 2x+2y=20, so y=10−x for 0≤x≤10. Area A=x(10−x), with A′=10−2x. The maximum occurs at x=5, y=5, with area 25 square units; at the degenerate boundaries area is 0.

Additional worked example

A 24 m fence forms three sides of a rectangle against a wall. Find the maximum area.

Let the two widths be x and the fenced length y. Then 2x+y=24, A=x(24−2x), 0≤x≤12. A′=24−4x gives x=6, y=12, area 72 m².

If it went wrong. Using four fenced sides would impose the wrong constraint and answer.

Optional visual explanationCallie Rethman · Maximizing Area ↗

lessons.title: Exponential and logarithmic rates
lessons.html:
20

Exponential and logarithmic rates

Idea

The exponential e^x is its own derivative. A logarithm turns multiplication into addition and has a reciprocal rate. With a changing exponent or argument, the chain rule is still required.

First move

Identify the inner expression and its derivative. For ln|u|, work where u≠0; for ln u, require u>0.

Worked reasoning

For y=e^(2x) ln x on x>0, the product rule gives y′=2e^(2x)ln x+e^(2x)/x=e^(2x)(2ln x+1/x).

Additional worked example

Differentiate y=ln(x²+1).

y′=2x/(x²+1); the argument is positive for every real x.

If it went wrong. The derivative is not 1/(x²+1); the inner derivative 2x is essential.

lessons.title: Logarithmic differentiation
lessons.html:
21

Logarithmic differentiation

Idea

Taking a logarithm can turn variable powers and products into simpler sums. State the positive-domain assumption or use absolute values where appropriate.

First move

For y=[u(x)]^[v(x)] with u>0, write ln y=v ln u, differentiate both sides, then multiply by y.

Worked reasoning

For y=x^x on x>0, ln y=x ln x. Hence y′/y=ln x+1 and y′=x^x(ln x+1).

Additional worked example

Differentiate y=(x²+1)^x.

ln y=x ln(x²+1), so y′=(x²+1)^x[ln(x²+1)+2x²/(x²+1)].

If it went wrong. Treating x as a constant exponent would omit the ln(x²+1) term.

lessons.title: Inverse trigonometric derivatives
lessons.html:
22

Inverse trigonometric derivatives

Idea

An inverse trigonometric derivative converts a rate of the input into a rate of angle. Its domain restrictions come from the inverse function and the displayed denominator.

First move

Use the correct inverse function rule and multiply by the derivative of the argument. For arcsin, note that the derivative is undefined at input ±1.

Worked reasoning

For y=arctan(2x), y′=2/(1+4x²). For y=arcsin(x²), y′=2x/√(1−x⁴), wherever |x|<1.

Additional worked example

Differentiate y=arctan(x³).

y′=3x²/(1+x⁶).

If it went wrong. Replacing arctan’s denominator with √(1−u²) confuses it with arcsin.

lessons.title: Reverse a derivative
lessons.html:
23

Reverse a derivative

Idea

An antiderivative is a family of functions with the given derivative. All members differ by a constant on an interval. The exponent −1 is a special logarithmic case.

First move

Apply reverse rules term by term, retain +C, then differentiate the result to verify it. Use initial data to determine C.

Worked reasoning

If F′(x)=6x²−4 and F(1)=5, then F(x)=2x³−4x+C. At x=1, 2−4+C=5, so C=7.

Additional worked example

Find F if F′(x)=3x²+2x and F(0)=−1.

F(x)=x³+x²−1; differentiating returns 3x²+2x.

If it went wrong. Without initial data, keep +C. With it, determine the unique member of the family.

Optional visual explanationNick Kaneko · Antiderivatives ↗

lessons.title: Core integral patterns
lessons.html:
24

Core integral patterns

Idea

Integration reverses known derivative pairs. The absolute value in ln|x| allows either nonzero sign of x on an interval. Trigonometric antiderivatives still assume radians.

First move

Match the integrand to a derivative you know. Differentiate the proposed answer to check sign and coefficient.

Worked reasoning

∫[2x+cos x+1/x] dx=x²+sin x+ln|x|+C on any interval avoiding zero.

Additional worked example

Find ∫[3x²−sin x] dx.

x³+cos x+C, because the derivative of cos x is −sin x.

If it went wrong. A sign error in integrating −sin x is easy to catch by differentiation.

lessons.title: Sums become accumulation
lessons.html:
25

Sums become accumulation

Idea

A Riemann sum adds height times width over many thin subintervals. The definite integral is signed accumulation; portions below the x-axis subtract rather than add.

First move

When given a sum, identify interval, width, and sample points. When asked for physical total distance or region area, use absolute values or split at crossings as needed.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x on [0,2], two equal left rectangles have heights 0 and 1, so their sum is 1. The right sum is 1+2=3. The exact integral is 2, between these estimates.

Additional worked example

Find the exact signed integral of f(x)=x on [−1,1], and its geometric area.

The signed integral is 0 because equal negative and positive triangles cancel. Geometric area is 1/2+1/2=1.

If it went wrong. Integral and geometric area differ when the function crosses the axis.

lessons.title: The two directions of the fundamental theorem
lessons.html:
26

The two directions of the fundamental theorem

Idea

Accumulation has derivative equal to the current rate when f is continuous. Conversely, an antiderivative evaluates total signed accumulation between bounds.

First move

If the upper bound is a function g(x), multiply by g′(x). If evaluating an integral, find F and compute upper minus lower, with parentheses.

Worked reasoning

For A(x)=∫₁^(x²) cos t dt, A′(x)=cos(x²)·2x. Also ∫₀² 3x² dx=[x³]₀²=8.

Additional worked example

Find d/dx of ∫₀^(3x) √(1+t²) dt.

3√(1+9x²), from evaluating the integrand at 3x and multiplying by 3.

If it went wrong. Omitting the derivative of a variable upper bound loses the chain-rule factor.

Optional visual explanationNick Kaneko · Fundamental Theorem, Part 1 ↗

lessons.title: Average value and substitution
lessons.html:
27

Average value and substitution

Idea

Average value is total accumulation divided by interval length. Substitution reverses the chain rule by replacing an inner function and its differential together.

First move

For a nested integrand, choose u as the inner expression. In a definite integral, change both bounds into u-values before integrating.

Worked reasoning

∫₀¹ 2x(1+x²)³ dx: let u=1+x², du=2x dx, and bounds become 1 and 2. Then ∫₁²u³ du=[u⁴/4]₁²=15/4.

Additional worked example

Find the average value of f(x)=x² on [0,2].

(1/2)∫₀²x² dx=(1/2)(8/3)=4/3.

If it went wrong. The integral alone is accumulated total. Divide by the interval length for the average.

Optional visual explanationCallie Rethman · Substitution with an Extra Variable ↗

lessons.title: Area between graphs
lessons.html:
28

Area between graphs

Idea

The height of a vertical strip is upper curve minus lower curve. If curves cross inside the interval, the strip order changes and the area integral must be split.

First move

Find intersections, identify which curve is above on each interval, integrate the positive difference, then add the pieces.

Worked reasoning

Between y=x and y=x² on [0,1], x≥x², so A=∫₀¹(x−x²)dx=[x²/2−x³/3]₀¹=1/6.

Additional worked example

Find the area between y=2x and y=x² from their intersections.

Intersections are x=0 and x=2. Since 2x≥x² there, area is ∫₀²(2x−x²)dx=4/3.

If it went wrong. Integrating lower minus upper gives a negative signed value, not the requested area.

Optional visual explanationCallie Rethman · Area Between Curves ↗

lessons.title: Disks and washers from cross sections
lessons.html:
29

Disks and washers from cross sections

Idea

Rotation of a vertical region about a horizontal axis produces circular cross sections perpendicular to that axis. Radius is distance from the axis, so identify outer and inner boundaries before squaring.

First move

Draw one representative slice. If the region touches the axis, the inner radius is zero; otherwise subtract the hole.

Worked reasoning

Rotate the region under y=x, 0≤x≤2, about the x-axis. Its disk radius is x, so V=π∫₀²x² dx=8π/3 cubic units.

Additional worked example

Rotate the region between y=2 and y=x, 0≤x≤2, about the x-axis. Find the volume.

Outer radius 2, inner radius x. V=π∫₀²(4−x²)dx=16π/3.

If it went wrong. Squaring the difference (2−x)² describes the wrong cross-sectional area; use R²−r².
