lessons.title: Functions and their graphs
lessons.html:
01

Functions and their graphs

Meaning

A function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input. Its domain is the allowed input set; its range is the outputs actually attained. A graph passes the vertical line test precisely when it represents a function of x.

Method

Read a graph in this order: domain, range, intercepts, sign, increasing or decreasing intervals, then symmetry. Compute f(−x): equality with f(x) means even symmetry; equality with −f(x) means odd symmetry. Neither relation may hold. For a formula, exclude zero denominators and negative radicands of even roots.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=√(4−x²), require 4−x²≥0, so the domain is [−2,2]. Outputs run from 0 to 2. Since f(−x)=f(x), the upper semicircle is even.

Additional worked example

Find the domain and symmetry of g(x)=x/(x²−1).

Exclude x=−1 and x=1. Since g(−x)=−g(x), the function is odd on its symmetric domain.

Common error. A vertical line crossing twice disproves function status; a horizontal line crossing twice does not.

lessons.title: Composition of functions
lessons.html:
02

Composition of functions

Meaning

Composition feeds the output of one function into another. Order matters, and the domain must survive both stages.

Method

Identify the inner operation first, then the outer operation. For the domain of f∘g, require x in the domain of g and g(x) in the domain of f. To unpack a complicated expression, peel off the outermost action one layer at a time.

Worked reasoning

If f(u)=√u and g(x)=x−3, then (f∘g)(x)=√(x−3), defined for x≥3. But (g∘f)(x)=√x−3, defined for x≥0; the outputs and domains differ.

Additional worked example

Write h(x)=ln(1+x²) as a composition and state its domain.

Take g(x)=1+x² and f(u)=ln u. Then h=f∘g. Because 1+x²>0 for every real x, the domain is all real numbers.

Common error. Do not cancel the distinction between f(g(x)) and g(f(x)); test each domain from inside outward.

lessons.title: Average and instantaneous change
lessons.html:
03

Average and instantaneous change

Meaning

Average change is the slope of a secant line across an interval. Instantaneous change is the limiting secant slope at one input, if that limit exists.

Method

Compute output change divided by input change and keep units: output units per input unit. To approach an instantaneous rate, replace the interval by [a,a+h], simplify while h≠0, and take h→0. The tangent slope can be positive, zero, or negative.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x² at x=2, the secant slope over [2,2+h] is [(2+h)²−4]/h=4+h. Its limit is 4.

Additional worked example

Find the average rate of f(x)=1/x on [2,4].

[(1/4)−(1/2)]/(4−2)=−1/8. The negative sign records decreasing output as x increases.

Common error. Never treat an average rate over a finite interval as the rate at either endpoint.

lessons.title: Investigating a limit
lessons.html:
04

Investigating a limit

Meaning

A limit describes what outputs approach near an input, not necessarily the output at that input. Both one-sided approaches must agree for a finite two-sided limit.

Method

Use a graph to see approach direction and a table of nearby inputs on both sides to estimate. Then seek an algebraic argument: numerical evidence alone can mislead near a sharp feature. Separate a hole, jump, vertical asymptote, and oscillation.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=(x²−4)/(x−2) with x≠2, nearby outputs approach 4 because f(x)=x+2 away from 2. The value f(2) remains undefined; the limit is 4.

Additional worked example

If f(x)=−1 for x<0 and f(x)=2 for x≥0, what is lim as x→0 of f(x)?

The left limit is −1 and the right limit is 2; the two-sided limit does not exist.

Common error. A table with values only on one side cannot establish a two-sided limit.

lessons.title: Algebraic limit methods
lessons.html:
05

Algebraic limit methods

Meaning

Direct substitution works when the expression remains continuous. An apparent 0/0 signals algebra to perform, not a numerical answer.

Method

Factor and cancel a common nonzero factor near the point; rationalize radicals; or divide by the dominant power for behavior at infinity. For a trigonometric limit, rewrite it to expose sin(u)/u and account for any scale factor. Use one-sided signs to analyze a denominator tending to zero without cancellation.

Worked reasoning

lim as x→3 of (x²−9)/(x−3) equals lim(x+3)=6 after factoring. In contrast, lim as x→∞ of (3x²−1)/(2x²+5)=3/2 after division by x².

Additional worked example

Evaluate lim as x→0 of sin(5x)/x.

Rewrite as 5[sin(5x)/(5x)]; the inner ratio tends to 1, so the limit is 5.

Common error. Cancellation is legal for x near the target, not at the point where the original denominator is zero.

lessons.title: Formal definition of a limit
lessons.html:
06

Formal definition of a limit

Meaning

The epsilon–delta definition makes “arbitrarily close” exact: every requested output tolerance ε>0 must admit an input tolerance δ>0.

Method

Start with |f(x)−L| and bound it by an expression containing |x−a|. Choose δ as a function of ε. When another factor varies with x, first keep x within a simple neighborhood such as |x−a|<1, then control the remaining factor.

Worked reasoning

To prove lim as x→3 of (2x+1)=7, observe |(2x+1)−7|=2|x−3|. Choosing δ=ε/2 makes 0<|x−3|<δ imply the required bound.

Additional worked example

Choose δ for lim as x→4 of (3x−2)=10.

Because |(3x−2)−10|=3|x−4|, δ=ε/3 works for every ε>0.

Common error. δ may depend on ε, but a proof cannot choose ε after choosing a particular x.

lessons.title: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem
lessons.html:
07

Continuity and the intermediate value theorem

Meaning

Continuity at a means f(a) exists, the limit exists, and they agree. For a continuous function on [a,b], every value between f(a) and f(b) is attained somewhere inside.

Method

Check domain and one-sided behavior before invoking continuity. A hole can be repaired by assigning the limiting value; a jump generally cannot. For an existence question, identify a continuous interval and show the target lies between endpoint outputs.

Worked reasoning

Let f(x)=x³−x−1. It is continuous. Since f(1)=−1 and f(2)=5, some c in (1,2) satisfies f(c)=0, even without an explicit root.

Additional worked example

Can the intermediate value theorem prove that x²−2 has a root between 1 and 2?

Yes. The polynomial is continuous, and its endpoint values are −1 and 2, so zero lies between them.

Common error. The theorem guarantees existence; it does not give a formula or prove uniqueness.

lessons.title: Derivative from its limit definition
lessons.html:
08

Derivative from its limit definition

Meaning

The derivative is the limit of difference quotients and represents local slope or instantaneous rate. Differentiability requires a finite common limit from both sides.

Method

Substitute f(a+h), subtract f(a), simplify the numerator, cancel h while h≠0, then take h→0. For radicals, multiply by the conjugate. At a corner or cusp, compare one-sided slopes.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=√x and a>0, [√(a+h)−√a]/h becomes 1/[√(a+h)+√a] after rationalization. Hence f′(a)=1/(2√a).

Additional worked example

Use the definition to find the derivative of f(x)=x²+1 at x=3.

The quotient is [(3+h)²+1−10]/h=6+h; its limit is 6.

Common error. Substituting h=0 before simplifying creates 0/0 and loses the limiting slope.

lessons.title: Power, constant, and sum rules
lessons.html:
09

Power, constant, and sum rules

Meaning

Power rules replace repeated limit calculations for polynomial, reciprocal, and radical powers wherever the expression is differentiable.

Method

Rewrite roots and reciprocals as exponents, differentiate each term, and retain constants as coefficients. A standalone constant has derivative zero. Check the original domain, since rewriting a negative power does not create a value at x=0.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=3x⁴−2√x+5/x, rewrite as 3x⁴−2x^(1/2)+5x^(−1). Then f′(x)=12x³−x^(−1/2)−5x^(−2), for x>0.

Additional worked example

Differentiate 4/x³−7x²+9.

Write 4x^(−3)−7x²+9. The derivative is −12x^(−4)−14x.

Common error. The exponent falls by one after multiplying by the original exponent; it does not simply fall by one.

lessons.title: Product rule
lessons.html:
10

Product rule

Meaning

Two changing factors contribute separately to the change in their product. A derivative of a product is generally not the product of derivatives.

Method

Label the factors before differentiating. Differentiate one while holding the other, then reverse and add. Expand first only when that makes the algebra simpler; both routes must agree.

Worked reasoning

For y=(x²+1)eˣ, y′=2xeˣ+(x²+1)eˣ=eˣ(x²+2x+1).

Additional worked example

Differentiate (x³−2)sin x.

3x² sin x+(x³−2)cos x.

Common error. Both product-rule terms must appear, even if one factor looks simple.

lessons.title: Quotient rule
lessons.html:
11

Quotient rule

Meaning

When a numerator and denominator both vary, their effects oppose one another in the derivative.

Method

Name numerator f and denominator g, write “denominator times numerator derivative minus numerator times denominator derivative,” and divide by g². Preserve parentheses in the numerator. If the denominator is a simple power, rewriting as a negative exponent may be shorter.

Worked reasoning

For y=(x²+1)/x, the quotient rule gives [2x·x−(x²+1)]/x²=(x²−1)/x². Rewriting y=x+1/x gives the same 1−1/x².

Additional worked example

Differentiate sin x / x, for x≠0.

[x cos x−sin x]/x².

Common error. The denominator is squared as a whole; changing the order in the numerator changes the sign.

lessons.title: Rates of change in context
lessons.html:
12

Rates of change in context

Meaning

A derivative inherits context and units. Position yields velocity; velocity yields acceleration. Speed is |velocity|, so direction and speed are distinct.

Method

Write the physical quantity as a function of time, differentiate, evaluate at the requested time, then report units. For landing or a turning point, solve the relevant equation first and reject times outside the physical domain.

Worked reasoning

If s(t)=80−16t² feet, then v(t)=−32t feet/second. The object reaches ground when 80−16t²=0, so t=√5 seconds; its impact velocity is −32√5 feet/second.

Additional worked example

For s(t)=t³−6t² meters, find velocity and acceleration at t=2 seconds.

v(t)=3t²−12t, so v(2)=−12 m/s. a(t)=6t−12, so a(2)=0 m/s².

Common error. A negative velocity means direction, not negative speed.

lessons.title: Derivatives of trigonometric functions
lessons.html:
13

Derivatives of trigonometric functions

Meaning

The basic trigonometric derivatives support repeated differentiation of oscillating quantities. These rules require angles measured in radians.

Method

Use the six basic derivatives, then apply product, quotient, or chain rules when trig functions are combined or composed. Derive tan x from sin x/cos x if the sec²x rule is forgotten.

Worked reasoning

For y=3sin x−2tan x, y′=3cos x−2sec²x. For y=sin(5x), the chain rule adds the inner derivative, giving 5cos(5x).

Additional worked example

Differentiate cot x+sec x.

−csc²x+sec x tan x.

Common error. The derivative of cos x is negative sin x; degree measure changes the formula.

lessons.title: Chain rule
lessons.html:
14

Chain rule

Meaning

A change in x first changes the inner expression, which then changes the outer function. Multiply those rates.

Method

Mark the outer layer and inner layer. Differentiate the outer form while leaving the inner expression in place, then multiply by the derivative of the inner. For multiple nested layers, repeat from outside inward.

Worked reasoning

For y=(1+3x²)⁵, y′=5(1+3x²)⁴·6x=30x(1+3x²)⁴. The factor 6x comes from the inside.

Additional worked example

Differentiate e^(x³) and sin²(2x).

The derivatives are 3x²e^(x³) and 4sin(2x)cos(2x), respectively.

Common error. If an outer derivative looks correct but lacks the inner derivative, the chain rule is incomplete.

lessons.title: Inverse trigonometric derivatives
lessons.html:
15

Inverse trigonometric derivatives

Meaning

An inverse trigonometric function returns an angle from a ratio. Its derivative is not the reciprocal of the corresponding trigonometric derivative.

Method

Choose the correct inverse derivative and apply the chain rule to its argument. Respect real-domain restrictions: arcsin u and arccos u require |u|≤1, and their derivatives fail at boundary points where the denominator vanishes.

Worked reasoning

For y=arctan(x²), y′=2x/(1+x⁴). The denominator uses the square of the full input x².

Additional worked example

Differentiate arcsin(3x) where |x|<1/3.

3/√(1−9x²).

Common error. The notation sin⁻¹x means arcsin x here, not 1/sin x.

lessons.title: Equation of a tangent line
lessons.html:
16

Equation of a tangent line

Meaning

A tangent line passes through (a,f(a)) with slope f′(a). Its local agreement with the curve is first order.

Method

Identify the requested x-coordinate a, evaluate f(a), compute f′(a), and insert both into point–slope form. Verify that the result passes through the point and has a plausible slope.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x² at a=3, the point is (3,9) and slope is 6. Thus y−9=6(x−3), or y=6x−9.

Additional worked example

Find the tangent line to y=eˣ at x=0.

The point is (0,1) and slope is 1, giving y=x+1.

Common error. The derivative value is the slope, not the y-coordinate of the tangency point.

lessons.title: Implicit differentiation
lessons.html:
17

Implicit differentiation

Meaning

A curve can define y without a simple explicit formula. Differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a changing function of x.

Method

Whenever a differentiated term contains y, apply the chain rule and include y′. Collect every y′ term, factor, and solve. A resulting slope may depend on both x and y; evaluate it at a point only after finding the general relation.

Worked reasoning

For x²+y²=25, differentiation gives 2x+2yy′=0, so y′=−x/y when y≠0. At (3,4), the tangent slope is −3/4.

Additional worked example

For xy=6, find y′.

Product rule gives y+xy′=0, hence y′=−y/x where x≠0.

Common error. Differentiating y² as 2y rather than 2yy′ silently treats y as a constant.

lessons.title: Higher derivatives
lessons.html:
18

Higher derivatives

Meaning

Repeated differentiation measures the change of a rate. For position, the second derivative is acceleration; in graphs, its sign indicates concavity.

Method

Differentiate one stage at a time and label each result. For periodic functions, find the derivative cycle before jumping to a high order. For e^(kx), each differentiation adds a factor k.

Worked reasoning

The derivative cycle of sin x is cos x, −sin x, −cos x, sin x. Hence the 101st derivative is cos x because 101 leaves remainder 1 upon division by 4.

Additional worked example

Find the fourth derivative of e^(2x).

Each step contributes a factor 2, so the result is 16e^(2x).

Common error. A second derivative is not the square of the first derivative.

lessons.title: Logarithmic and exponential derivatives
lessons.html:
19

Logarithmic and exponential derivatives

Meaning

Exponential differentiation reproduces the exponential while logarithmic differentiation converts products and powers into sums and coefficients.

Method

Use chain rule for an exponential or logarithm of an expression. For y=xˣ with x>0, take natural logs: ln y=x ln x; differentiate implicitly and multiply back by y. For a positive base a≠1, aˣ=e^(x ln a).

Worked reasoning

For y=xˣ, y′/y=ln x+1, so y′=xˣ(ln x+1). For ln(x²+1), the derivative is 2x/(x²+1).

Additional worked example

Differentiate 3^(2x).

The derivative is 2 ln(3)·3^(2x).

Common error. The derivative of ln|u| is u′/u only where u≠0; do not discard a chain factor.

lessons.title: Hyperbolic and inverse hyperbolic derivatives
lessons.html:
20

Hyperbolic and inverse hyperbolic derivatives

Meaning

Hyperbolic functions are built from exponentials. Their derivatives resemble trig derivatives but some signs differ: (cosh x)′=sinh x, without a minus sign.

Method

Apply the basic derivative and then the chain rule. For inverse hyperbolic tangent, use (artanh u)′=u′/(1−u²), valid in the real interval |u|<1. Check the argument domain before evaluating.

Worked reasoning

For y=[artanh(x²)]³ on |x|<1, y′=3[artanh(x²)]²·2x/(1−x⁴).

Additional worked example

Differentiate sinh(3x)+cosh x.

3cosh(3x)+sinh x.

Common error. Do not import the minus sign from the derivative of ordinary cosine into hyperbolic cosine.

lessons.title: Related rates
lessons.html:
21

Related rates

Meaning

Related rates connect several quantities changing with time through one geometric or physical equation.

Method

Draw and label a diagram; write a relation between variables; differentiate with respect to time before inserting the instant’s measurements; solve for the requested rate and state units and direction. If the geometry changes width, a constant input volume rate need not produce a constant height rate.

Worked reasoning

For a sphere at radius 5 ft expanding at 0.1 ft/min, dV/dt=4π(5)²(0.1)=10π ft³/min.

Additional worked example

A circle radius grows at 2 cm/s. How quickly does area grow when radius is 3 cm?

A=πr², so dA/dt=2πr(dr/dt)=12π cm²/s.

Common error. Substituting r before differentiating can incorrectly turn a changing quantity into a constant.

lessons.title: Linear approximation and differentials
lessons.html:
22

Linear approximation and differentials

Meaning

Near a known point, the tangent line gives a simple estimate for a smooth curve. The approximation improves as x approaches a.

Method

Choose a nearby a where f(a) and f′(a) are easy. Set Δx=x−a and estimate Δf≈f′(a)Δx. Check whether the estimate’s direction is sensible and remember that the neglected curvature creates error.

Worked reasoning

For √1.08, use f(x)=√x at a=1. Then f(1)=1 and f′(1)=1/2, so √1.08≈1+(1/2)(0.08)=1.04.

Additional worked example

Estimate ∛8.12 using a=8.

For f(x)=x^(1/3), f(8)=2 and f′(8)=1/12. With Δx=0.12, the estimate is 2+0.12/12=2.01.

Common error. A tangent-line estimate is local; using a faraway a can make it poor.

lessons.title: Absolute extrema on an interval
lessons.html:
23

Absolute extrema on an interval

Meaning

An absolute maximum or minimum is the largest or smallest attained function value over a domain. A critical point is an interior point where f′=0 or f′ does not exist.

Method

For a continuous function on a closed interval, compute f at both endpoints and at every interior critical point; compare the outputs. On open or unbounded intervals, check limiting behavior and whether a bound is actually attained.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x²−4x on [0,5], f′=2x−4 vanishes at x=2. Values are f(0)=0, f(2)=−4, f(5)=5. Thus the absolute minimum is −4 and maximum is 5.

Additional worked example

Find the absolute extrema of f(x)=x(4−x) on [0,4].

f′=4−2x=0 at x=2. The values are 0, 4, 0, so the maximum is 4 at x=2 and minimum is 0 at both endpoints.

Common error. A zero derivative yields a candidate, not proof of an absolute extreme.

lessons.title: Mean value theorem and Rolle’s theorem
lessons.html:
24

Mean value theorem and Rolle’s theorem

Meaning

If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), some tangent slope equals the interval’s secant slope. Rolle’s theorem is the special case f(a)=f(b), giving f′(c)=0.

Method

Verify continuity, differentiability, and endpoint values first. Compute the secant slope, solve f′(c)=that slope, and keep only solutions strictly inside (a,b). A corner or gap can invalidate the theorem even if the endpoint values match.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x² on [1,3], the secant slope is (9−1)/2=4. Since f′(x)=2x, c=2 satisfies the theorem.

Additional worked example

Apply Rolle’s theorem to f(x)=x²−4 on [−2,2]. Find c.

The endpoint values are both 0 and the polynomial is smooth. f′(x)=2x, so c=0.

Common error. The theorem guarantees a c inside the interval only after its hypotheses are checked.

lessons.title: First and second derivative tests
lessons.html:
25

First and second derivative tests

Meaning

The sign of f′ tells whether a curve rises or falls. The sign of f″ tells concavity and can classify a stationary point when f″ is nonzero.

Method

Find critical points, split the domain into intervals, and test the sign of f′ on each. At a point with f′=0, f″>0 implies a local minimum and f″<0 a local maximum. If f″=0, return to the first derivative test or another argument.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x³−3x, f′=3(x−1)(x+1). It changes + to − at −1 (local maximum) and − to + at 1 (local minimum).

Additional worked example

Classify the stationary point of f(x)=x⁴ at x=0.

f″(0)=0 is inconclusive, but f′=4x³ changes from negative to positive, so x=0 is a local minimum.

Common error. f″=0 does not mean “no extremum”; it means the second derivative test did not decide.

lessons.title: L’Hôpital’s rule
lessons.html:
26

L’Hôpital’s rule

Meaning

For a quotient with a verified 0/0 or ∞/∞ form, differentiating numerator and denominator separately can reveal its limit, under the rule’s conditions.

Method

Determine the form before applying the rule. Differentiate top and bottom independently, then re-evaluate; repeat only if the new quotient remains indeterminate. Transform products, differences, and variable powers into a quotient or take logarithms before using the rule.

Worked reasoning

lim as x→0 of (eˣ−1)/x is 0/0, then lim eˣ/1=1. This is not a quotient-rule differentiation.

Additional worked example

Evaluate lim as x→∞ of x/eˣ.

It is ∞/∞, so one application gives lim 1/eˣ=0.

Common error. The rule does not apply to a quotient merely because a denominator approaches zero.

lessons.title: Curve sketching from evidence
lessons.html:
27

Curve sketching from evidence

Meaning

A reliable sketch combines domain, intercepts, asymptotes, symmetry, increasing or decreasing intervals, extrema, and concavity.

Method

Start with the domain and boundary behavior. Calculate intercepts and possible symmetry. Use sign charts for f′ and f″; mark critical and inflection candidates only after checking actual sign changes. Plot a few exact points and join them without crossing excluded inputs.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x³−3x, the odd graph crosses at −√3, 0, √3. f′=3x²−3 gives a local maximum at −1 and minimum at 1. f″=6x changes sign at 0, giving an inflection point there.

Additional worked example

For f(x)=1/x, state domain, symmetry, and asymptotes.

Domain x≠0; f(−x)=−f(x), so odd symmetry. x=0 is a vertical asymptote and y=0 a horizontal asymptote.

Common error. f″=0 is an inflection candidate; verify a concavity change before labeling it.

lessons.title: Applied optimization
lessons.html:
28

Applied optimization

Meaning

Optimization turns a real constraint into a one-variable objective, then uses derivative evidence to choose a feasible best value.

Method

Sketch and label variables, write the objective, use constraints to eliminate variables, determine the physical domain, find critical points, compare with boundaries, then translate the winning x back into the requested dimensions or quantity.

Worked reasoning

A 12-by-12 sheet forms an open box by cutting x from each corner. V(x)=x(12−2x)² for 0<x<6. V′=12(x−2)(x−6); the interior maximum is at x=2, giving V=128 cubic units.

Additional worked example

A rectangle has perimeter 20. What dimensions maximize its area?

Let one side be x; the other is 10−x, with 0<x<10. A=x(10−x), and A′=10−2x vanishes at x=5. The maximum is a 5-by-5 square.

Common error. An algebraic critical point outside the feasible domain cannot solve the original problem.

lessons.title: Newton’s method
lessons.html:
29

Newton’s method

Meaning

Newton’s method uses a tangent-line x-intercept to refine a root estimate for f(x)=0.

Method

Choose an initial estimate near the desired root. Evaluate f and f′ at that estimate and iterate. Stop when the change and residual are suitably small. If f′ is zero or very small, or the starting point is poor, the iteration may fail or move to a different root.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x²−2 and x₀=1.5, x₁=1.5−(2.25−2)/3=1.41667. One further step gives approximately 1.41422, close to √2.

Additional worked example

Use one Newton step for f(x)=x²−3 from x₀=2.

x₁=2−(4−3)/4=1.75.

Common error. An iteration value is an approximation; check the residual f(xₙ) rather than assuming convergence.

lessons.title: Approximate area and distance
lessons.html:
30

Approximate area and distance

Meaning

A rectangle sum approximates accumulated area. With velocity as the height, the sum approximates displacement; absolute velocity approximates distance traveled.

Method

Partition [a,b] into equal widths. Select left endpoints, right endpoints, or midpoints as sample positions; multiply each height by width and add. For an increasing positive function, left sums underestimate and right sums overestimate. A midpoint estimate is often better but is not universally exact.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x on [0,2] with two equal rectangles, Δx=1. Left sum is f(0)+f(1)=1; right sum is f(1)+f(2)=3; midpoint sum is f(0.5)+f(1.5)=2.

Additional worked example

Compute L₂ and R₂ for f(x)=x² on [0,2].

With Δx=1, L₂=f(0)+f(1)=1 and R₂=f(1)+f(2)=5.

Common error. Do not omit Δx; summing heights alone has the wrong units.

lessons.title: Riemann sums and the fundamental theorem
lessons.html:
31

Riemann sums and the fundamental theorem

Meaning

A definite integral is the limit of signed rectangle sums. The fundamental theorem links this accumulation to antiderivatives.

Method

Interpret ∫ as signed area or accumulated change. To evaluate, find an antiderivative F and subtract F(a) from F(b). Reversing bounds changes the sign; adjacent intervals add. If an accumulation function is A(x)=∫ from a to x of f(t)dt, then A′(x)=f(x) where f is continuous.

Worked reasoning

∫ from 0 to 2 of (3x²−1)dx = [x³−x] from 0 to 2 = 6. The integrand may be negative on part of the interval, but the integral is net signed accumulation.

Additional worked example

Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of 2x dx.

An antiderivative is x²; 3²−1²=8.

Common error. A definite integral can be negative; “area” without qualification is not always the same as signed integral.

lessons.title: Substitution in integration
lessons.html:
32

Substitution in integration

Meaning

Substitution reverses the chain rule by replacing a repeated inner expression with a new variable.

Method

Set u equal to the inner expression, compute du, and rewrite the entire integrand. For a definite integral, convert both bounds to u-values or return to x before evaluating, never mix systems. Differentiate an indefinite result to check.

Worked reasoning

∫2x cos(x²)dx: let u=x², du=2x dx. Then ∫cos u du=sin u+C=sin(x²)+C.

Additional worked example

Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 1 of 2x/(1+x²) dx.

Set u=1+x², giving bounds 1 to 2. The integral is ∫ from 1 to 2 of du/u = ln 2.

Common error. Replacing g(x) by u while leaving an unmatched x or dx behind is not a completed substitution.

lessons.title: Area between curves
lessons.html:
33

Area between curves

Meaning

Thin strips add vertical or horizontal gaps between boundaries. Geometric area is nonnegative, so a crossing may require splitting an interval.

Method

Find intersections to establish bounds. Decide whether vertical or horizontal strips describe the region more simply. For vertical strips integrate top minus bottom with respect to x; for horizontal strips integrate right minus left with respect to y. Split where the ordering changes.

Worked reasoning

Between y=x and y=x² on [0,1], x≥x², so A=∫₀¹(x−x²)dx=[x²/2−x³/3]₀¹=1/6.

Additional worked example

Find the area enclosed by y=4 and y=x².

Intersections are x=−2 and 2. A=∫₋₂²(4−x²)dx=32/3.

Common error. Integrating one curve alone gives area to the axis, not necessarily area between two curves.

lessons.title: Volumes by disks and washers
lessons.html:
34

Volumes by disks and washers

Meaning

Slices perpendicular to the rotation axis are circles or rings. Each cross-sectional area is π times outer radius squared minus inner radius squared.

Method

Sketch the region and axis. Pick a slice perpendicular to the axis, measure outer and inner radii as distances from the axis, then integrate cross-sectional area across the full solid. A disk is a washer with inner radius zero.

Worked reasoning

Rotate the region under y=x, 0≤x≤2, about the x-axis. Each disk has radius x, so V=π∫₀²x²dx=8π/3.

Additional worked example

Rotate the region between y=2 and y=1, 0≤x≤3, about the x-axis. Find the volume.

Outer radius 2 and inner radius 1 give V=π∫₀³(4−1)dx=9π.

Common error. A radius is distance to the rotation axis, not automatically the displayed function value.

lessons.title: Volumes by cylindrical shells
lessons.html:
35

Volumes by cylindrical shells

Meaning

Slices parallel to the rotation axis sweep out thin cylindrical shells. Circumference times height times thickness gives each shell’s volume.

Method

Draw a representative strip parallel to the axis. Radius is its distance to the axis; height is upper minus lower or right minus left; thickness fixes whether the integration variable is x or y. Compare with washers and choose the setup with simpler boundaries.

Worked reasoning

Rotate the region under y=x on [0,2] about the y-axis. Vertical strips have radius x and height x, so V=2π∫₀²x²dx=16π/3.

Additional worked example

Rotate the region under y=1 on [0,2] about the y-axis. Use shells.

Radius x, height 1; V=2π∫₀²x dx=4π.

Common error. The shell radius and height are different geometric measurements; do not square the radius as in a disk.

lessons.title: Average value of a function
lessons.html:
36

Average value of a function

Meaning

Average value is total signed accumulation divided by interval length. For a continuous function, some point in the interval attains this average.

Method

Compute the definite integral, then divide by b−a. Keep it distinct from the endpoint average [f(a)+f(b)]/2, which is generally different. If the function represents a rate, the average is a rate with the original output units.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x³ on [0,2], the integral is [x⁴/4]₀²=4. Dividing by interval length 2 gives average value 2.

Additional worked example

Find the average value of sin x on [0,π].

∫₀^π sin x dx=2, so the average is 2/π.

Common error. The integral itself is accumulated total; the average requires division by interval length.

lessons.title: Reading graphs of f, f′, and f″
lessons.html:
37

Reading graphs of f, f′, and f″

Meaning

The graph of f′ records slopes of f. The graph of f″ records slopes of f′ and concavity of f.

Method

Where f rises, plot f′ above the axis; where f falls, plot it below. Mark f′=0 at smooth horizontal tangents. Then apply the same slope reading to f′ to obtain f″. At a corner, f′ may be undefined, so do not draw a false zero.

Worked reasoning

For f(x)=x², slopes are negative left of zero, zero at zero, positive right of zero. Thus f′(x)=2x crosses the axis at zero; f″(x)=2 is positive everywhere.

Additional worked example

If f′ is positive but decreasing on an interval, what can be said about f and f″?

f is increasing, while f″ is negative (where defined), so its graph is concave down.

Common error. Positive f″ does not mean positive f; it means the slope f′ is increasing.

lessons.title: Slope fields
lessons.html:
38

Slope fields

Meaning

A differential equation supplies a slope at each point where its right-hand side is defined. A slope field shows short line segments with those slopes.

Method

Evaluate F at a grid of points and draw a short segment at each, without connecting points automatically. A solution curve follows the segments from its initial condition. Look for zero-slope lines and undefined regions before sketching.

Worked reasoning

For y′=x, all points with the same x share the same slope. Integrating gives y=x²/2+C; through (0,2), C=2.

Additional worked example

For y′=y−x, what is the slope along y=x?

It is zero because y−x=0 along that line; field marks there are horizontal.

Common error. A field segment is local slope information, not a straight solution line through the whole plane.

lessons.title: Separable equations and exponential change
lessons.html:
39

Separable equations and exponential change

Meaning

A separable equation factors into a y-part and an x-part. When growth rate is proportional to the current amount, solutions are exponential.

Method

For y′=ky, write dy/y=k dx on a region where y≠0, integrate to ln|y|=kx+C, and recover y=Ce^(kx). Include the zero solution, which division by y temporarily omits. Apply the initial condition; a positive k grows and negative k decays.

Worked reasoning

For y′=−0.03y with y(0)=500, y=500e^(−0.03x). Its half-life solves 1/2=e^(−0.03x), so x=ln2/0.03≈23.1 time units.

Additional worked example

Solve y′=0.05y, y(0)=100, and find doubling time.

y=100e^(0.05x). Doubling requires 2=e^(0.05x), so x=ln2/0.05≈13.9 time units.

Common error. Dividing by y without restoring y=0 can discard a valid solution.

lessons.title: Measurement and dimensional reasoning
lessons.html:
01

Measurement and dimensional reasoning

When you see

A quantity is reported in unfamiliar units or a proposed equation looks suspicious.

Choose this model

Quantity with dimensions; idealized particle or system only after the units are clear.

Principle

An equation can add only quantities of the same dimension. A unit check can reject an equation but cannot establish that the physical model is true. Keep extra digits until the final reported answer.

First move

Cancel units explicitly, estimate the expected scale, and report precision supported by the given data.

Worked reasoning

72 km/h is 72/3.6 = 20 m/s. At constant speed for 5 s, the distance is 100 m.

Additional worked example

Convert 54 km/h to m/s, then find its constant-speed travel in 4 s.

15 m/s and 60 m. The conversion lowers the numerical speed because one metre per second is a larger unit than one kilometre per hour.

Important distinction. A dimensionally valid equation can still describe the wrong situation; state the physical condition before substitution.

lessons.title: Vectors, components, and products
lessons.html:
02

Vectors, components, and products

When you see

Several displacements or forces point in different directions, or work and torque appear.

Choose this model

Vector with signed components in a declared coordinate system.

Principle

Vectors add component by component. The dot product selects the component parallel to a second vector; the cross product measures a perpendicular turning effect and has a direction.

First move

Draw the axes and angle first. Check the quadrant before taking an inverse tangent. Keep units attached to each component.

Worked reasoning

A 3 m east displacement followed by 4 m north has components (3,4) m and magnitude 5 m, directed about 53 degrees north of east.

Additional worked example

Combine a 5 N east force and a 12 N north force.

Components are (5,12) N; magnitude is 13 N. The direction is about 67 degrees north of east.

Important distinction. Adding magnitudes would give 17 N and ignore direction. A negative component is not a negative magnitude.

lessons.title: Motion graphs and rates
lessons.html:
03

Motion graphs and rates

When you see

The question gives position, velocity, or acceleration as a graph or function of time.

Choose this model

Particle; choose a graph slope for a rate and a signed area for accumulation.

Principle

The slope of a position graph is velocity. The slope of a velocity graph is acceleration. Signed area under velocity gives displacement; absolute area gives distance.

First move

Mark the time interval and axis units. For a piecewise graph, calculate each signed area before adding.

Worked reasoning

A velocity of +4 m/s for 3 s, then -2 m/s for 2 s, gives displacement 12-4 = 8 m and distance 12+4 = 16 m.

Additional worked example

Velocity is -3 m/s for 4 s. Find displacement and distance.

Displacement is -12 m; distance is 12 m. The sign records direction, not the amount of ground covered.

Important distinction. The area under a position-time graph is not generally a displacement.

lessons.title: Constant acceleration and free fall
lessons.html:
04

Constant acceleration and free fall

When you see

Acceleration is constant over the entire interval, including ideal vertical motion near Earth.

Choose this model

Particle under constant acceleration.

Principle

These relationships follow from constant acceleration. For upward-positive free fall, a_y = -g even at the top of the path.

First move

Declare the positive axis, write initial and final states, and choose the relation that eliminates the unneeded variable.

Worked reasoning

A cart starts at 2 m/s and accelerates at 3 m/s² for 4 s. It ends at 14 m/s and moves 2(4)+0.5(3)(4²)=32 m.

Additional worked example

A ball is launched upward at 20 m/s. With g = 10 m/s², when does it first reach its highest point?

Set vertical velocity to zero: 0=20-10t, so t=2 s. Acceleration is still -10 m/s² at that instant.

Important distinction. Do not apply a constant-acceleration formula across intervals with changing acceleration.

lessons.title: Projectiles in two dimensions
lessons.html:
05

Projectiles in two dimensions

When you see

A body moves after launch while gravity is the only appreciable force.

Choose this model

Particle with independent horizontal and vertical equations sharing one time.

Principle

Ideal projectile motion has horizontal acceleration zero and vertical acceleration -g. A zero vertical velocity at the peak does not make the total velocity zero.

First move

Split launch velocity into components. Solve the vertical condition for time, then use that same time horizontally.

Worked reasoning

A ball leaves a 20 m ledge horizontally at 5 m/s. With g=10 m/s², falling takes 2 s and the horizontal range is 10 m.

Additional worked example

From a 45 m ledge, a ball launches horizontally at 8 m/s. Use g=10 m/s². Find its flight time and range.

Vertical fall gives 45=5t², hence t=3 s. Range is 8(3)=24 m.

Important distinction. The familiar equal-height range formula does not apply when launch and landing heights differ.

lessons.title: Relative motion
lessons.html:
06

Relative motion

When you see

The velocity of one object is described from a moving vehicle, river, or observer.

Choose this model

Particle velocities with frame labels; add vectors, not just speeds.

Principle

Relative velocity is a difference between observations in two frames. Frame labels make the chaining rule unambiguous.

First move

Name the moving object and each observer. Draw component arrows before solving for magnitude and heading.

Worked reasoning

A boat moves 4 m/s east relative to water, and water moves 3 m/s north relative to shore. The boat moves 5 m/s relative to shore, northeast.

Additional worked example

A walker moves 2 m/s east on a train moving 10 m/s east relative to ground. Find walker speed relative to ground.

12 m/s east. The two relative velocities add because their directions agree.

Important distinction. A velocity without its reference frame is incomplete.

lessons.title: Free-body diagrams and Newton laws
lessons.html:
07

Free-body diagrams and Newton laws

When you see

The target is an acceleration, contact force, or equilibrium condition.

Choose this model

One isolated body with only real external forces; particle under net force.

Principle

A net force changes velocity. Zero net force means zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity. Third-law partners act on different bodies.

First move

Choose one body, draw gravity and each contact or applied force, then resolve the sum on chosen axes.

Worked reasoning

A 4 kg cart has 18 N right and 6 N left. Its net force is 12 N right and its acceleration is 3 m/s² right.

Additional worked example

A 5 kg object has 25 N east and 10 N west. Find its acceleration.

Net force is 15 N east, so acceleration is 3 m/s² east.

Important distinction. Do not place an equal-and-opposite third-law partner on the same free-body diagram.

lessons.title: Friction and inclined surfaces
lessons.html:
08

Friction and inclined surfaces

When you see

A body touches a rough surface or moves along a slope.

Choose this model

One body with normal force and friction; decide rest versus sliding first.

Principle

Static friction adjusts up to a maximum; kinetic friction has approximate magnitude μkN while surfaces slide. The normal force is set by perpendicular force balance, not by a universal N=mg rule.

First move

Choose axes parallel and perpendicular to the slope. Use the impending-motion test before selecting a friction law.

Worked reasoning

For a 2 kg block sliding down a 30-degree slope with μk=0.20 and g=10, N≈17.3 N, downhill gravity is 10 N, friction is 3.46 N uphill, and a≈3.27 m/s² downhill.

Additional worked example

A 3 kg block rests on a horizontal floor with μs=0.5 and g=10. Can static friction hold against a 12 N horizontal pull?

Yes. N=30 N and the maximum static friction is 15 N, but actual static friction is 12 N, opposite the pull.

Important distinction. Setting static friction equal to μsN in every stationary problem overstates it.

lessons.title: Circular motion and inward force
lessons.html:
09

Circular motion and inward force

When you see

A trajectory bends, even when speed stays constant.

Choose this model

Particle with radial acceleration; identify the real force that supplies net inward force.

Principle

Centripetal acceleration is a direction of net acceleration, not an additional force. Tangential acceleration changes speed; radial acceleration changes direction.

First move

Point the radial axis toward the center. Resolve gravity, tension, friction, and normal force along it.

Worked reasoning

A 2 kg mass at 4 m/s on a 2 m radius needs 16 N net inward force.

Additional worked example

At twice the speed and the same radius and mass, how does required inward force change?

It becomes four times larger because mv²/r depends on speed squared.

Important distinction. A constant speed on a curved path is accelerated motion.

lessons.title: Resistive force and terminal speed
lessons.html:
10

Resistive force and terminal speed

When you see

Drag grows with speed and eventually balances a driving force.

Choose this model

Particle with a velocity-dependent force; terminal state has zero net force.

Principle

Drag opposes relative motion through a fluid. Linear and quadratic forms describe different regimes and cannot be interchanged without evidence.

First move

State the drag law. Balance weight and drag only at terminal speed; during approach to that speed acceleration remains nonzero.

Worked reasoning

For a 1 kg falling body with linear drag b=2 N·s/m and g=10, mg=bvt gives vt=5 m/s.

Additional worked example

For linear drag with m=2 kg, b=4 N·s/m, and g=10, find terminal speed.

vt=mg/b=20/4=5 m/s. This is a limiting speed, not the initial speed.

Important distinction. Zero acceleration at terminal speed does not mean that gravity has disappeared.

lessons.title: Work by constant and changing forces
lessons.html:
11

Work by constant and changing forces

When you see

A force acts over a displacement, possibly with a changing magnitude.

Choose this model

System energy transfer by work; integrate only the force component along motion.

Principle

Work is positive, negative, or zero according to the angle between force and displacement. Net work changes kinetic energy.

First move

Choose a system. For constant force use Fd cosφ; for changing force take signed area under F versus displacement.

Worked reasoning

Stretching a spring from 0 to 0.20 m with k=100 N/m stores 0.5kx²=2 J, supplied by 2 J of external quasistatic work.

Additional worked example

A net 12 N force acts along 3 m of motion. How much does kinetic energy change?

ΔK=Wnet=12(3)=36 J. Direction alignment is assumed.

Important distinction. A force perpendicular to instantaneous motion does zero instantaneous work despite changing direction.

lessons.title: System choice and energy conservation
lessons.html:
12

System choice and energy conservation

When you see

A height, spring compression, or speed changes without a need to find elapsed time.

Choose this model

System energy accounting; isolated for energy only when transfer across its boundary is negligible.

Principle

Energy is conserved overall. Mechanical energy K+U is constant only when nonconservative transfer and other exchange are absent. Potential energy belongs to an interacting system.

First move

Draw initial and final states, choose the system boundary, list transfers, then solve symbolically before inserting numbers.

Worked reasoning

A body released from rest drops 5 m with negligible drag. With g=10, mgh=0.5mv² gives v=10 m/s, independent of mass.

Additional worked example

A body falls 1.8 m from rest with g=10 and negligible drag. Find speed.

v=sqrt(2gh)=sqrt(36)=6 m/s. If drag matters, the mechanical-energy result overpredicts speed.

Important distinction. Do not call mechanical energy conserved when friction converts part of it to internal energy.

lessons.title: Power and efficiency
lessons.html:
13

Power and efficiency

When you see

The question asks how fast energy is transferred or how much input is useful.

Choose this model

Rate of work or energy flow across the chosen system boundary.

Principle

Power is a rate, not an amount of energy. At constant speed the driving power balances dissipative energy transfer at that instant.

First move

Compute output and input over the same interval. Separate joules from watts and state whether force and velocity are aligned.

Worked reasoning

A motor exerts 100 N along a vehicle moving at 3 m/s, so the instantaneous mechanical power is 300 W.

Additional worked example

A device receives 500 J and delivers 350 J of useful work. Find its efficiency.

η=350/500=0.70, or 70%. The remaining 150 J is transferred in other forms.

Important distinction. A force magnitude times speed is not the power if the force is oblique; use the dot product.

lessons.title: Momentum and impulse
lessons.html:
14

Momentum and impulse

When you see

A force acts briefly or an object rebounds.

Choose this model

Particle or system with momentum change caused by external impulse.

Principle

Impulse is the area under force versus time. It changes vector momentum. A short interaction can produce large average force without a large time interval.

First move

Use signed initial and final velocities. Compute Δp first, then divide by duration for average force if needed.

Worked reasoning

A 0.5 kg ball changes from +6 to -2 m/s. Its impulse is 0.5(-2-6)=-4 N·s.

Additional worked example

If that reversal lasts 0.020 s, what is average force on the ball?

Favg=J/Δt=-4/0.020=-200 N. The negative sign gives direction.

Important distinction. A bounce reverses momentum direction; subtract signed values instead of subtracting speeds.

lessons.title: Collisions and center of mass
lessons.html:
15

Collisions and center of mass

When you see

Bodies interact strongly with each other over a short time.

Choose this model

Multi-body system with negligible external impulse; kinetic energy requires its own test.

Principle

Internal collision forces cancel in system momentum accounting. Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy too; bodies that stick generally do not.

First move

Draw before and after velocity arrows. Conserve x and y momentum separately, then test energy only if the collision type warrants it.

Worked reasoning

A 1 kg cart at +4 m/s sticks to a stationary 3 kg cart. Shared velocity is +1 m/s. Kinetic energy falls from 8 J to 2 J.

Additional worked example

A 1 kg mass is at x=0 and a 3 kg mass at x=4 m. Find the center of mass.

xcm=(1·0+3·4)/4=3 m, closer to the heavier mass.

Important distinction. Momentum conservation is a system claim; it fails if external impulse during the event is substantial.

lessons.title: Variable-mass motion
lessons.html:
16

Variable-mass motion

When you see

A rocket ejects mass while gaining speed.

Choose this model

Rocket plus exhaust system; compare momentum before and after a short ejection.

Principle

In the ideal rocket model, expelled mass carries momentum opposite the rocket acceleration. The formula assumes constant exhaust speed relative to the rocket and negligible external force over the burn.

First move

Identify initial and final rocket mass, distinguish exhaust speed from rocket speed, and check that mi>mf produces positive speed gain.

Worked reasoning

If a rocket halves its mass and ejects gas at 2 km/s relative to itself, ideal speed gain is 2 ln2≈1.39 km/s.

Additional worked example

If the same ideal rocket reduces mass from 4 units to 1 unit, express its speed gain in terms of ve.

Δv=ve ln4≈1.386ve. A fourfold mass ratio does not yield four times the exhaust speed.

Important distinction. Do not treat mass as constant in F=ma while fuel is being expelled across the system boundary.

lessons.title: Angular kinematics
lessons.html:
17

Angular kinematics

When you see

A wheel turns and angular acceleration is given.

Choose this model

Rigid body rotating about a fixed axis.

Principle

Angular position, velocity, and acceleration parallel linear kinematics only when angular acceleration is constant. Points on a rigid wheel share ω but have different linear speeds.

First move

Work in radians, choose positive rotation, and use r to connect angular and tangential quantities.

Worked reasoning

Starting at 2 rad/s with α=3 rad/s² for 4 s, a wheel reaches 14 rad/s and turns through 32 rad.

Additional worked example

At ω=6 rad/s, what is tangential speed at r=0.50 m?

vt=rω=3 m/s. A point at twice the radius would have twice this speed.

Important distinction. Do not put degrees directly into equations derived using radians.

lessons.title: Torque and rotational inertia
lessons.html:
18

Torque and rotational inertia

When you see

An off-center force changes a rigid body’s rotation.

Choose this model

Rigid object under net torque about a specified fixed axis.

Principle

Torque depends on perpendicular lever arm. Moment of inertia depends on how mass is distributed relative to the axis, not just total mass.

First move

Mark the axis, determine each torque sign, and compute the relevant I. The torque equation is about the chosen fixed axis.

Worked reasoning

For a uniform disk with M=2 kg and R=0.50 m, I=0.5MR²=0.25 kg·m². A 1 N·m net torque gives α=4 rad/s².

Additional worked example

What torque is needed to accelerate an I=0.40 kg·m² wheel at 5 rad/s²?

τnet=Iα=2 N·m.

Important distinction. A force directed along the radius has zero torque about the center even if its magnitude is large.

lessons.title: Rolling and rotational energy
lessons.html:
19

Rolling and rotational energy

When you see

A wheel or ball both translates and rotates without slipping.

Choose this model

Rigid object with translation plus rotation; contact point instantaneously at rest relative to ground.

Principle

No-slip rolling links center-of-mass speed to angular speed. Static friction may enable rolling while doing no work at an ideal stationary contact point.

First move

Write both energy terms and the no-slip constraint. Do not replace a rotating body with a particle if its spin energy matters.

Worked reasoning

A uniform disk rolls from rest through a vertical drop h without dissipative loss. With I=0.5MR², Mgh=0.75Mv², so v=sqrt(4gh/3).

Additional worked example

For h=0.30 m and g=10 m/s², find the disk speed.

v=sqrt(4·10·0.30/3)=2 m/s. A frictionless sliding particle would reach sqrt(6) m/s.

Important distinction. The relation v=Rω fails for a wheel that slips.

lessons.title: Angular momentum
lessons.html:
20

Angular momentum

When you see

Rotation changes as mass moves inward, or an external torque acts for a time.

Choose this model

Rotating system; external torque changes angular momentum about the same axis.

Principle

Angular momentum is conserved when external torque about the selected axis is negligible. A changing moment of inertia can therefore change angular speed.

First move

State the axis and system before using Iiωi=Ifωf. Do not transfer a scalar relation to a problem with changing rotation direction.

Worked reasoning

A skater has I=4 kg·m² and ω=2 rad/s. Pulling arms inward to I=2 kg·m² gives ω=4 rad/s when external torque is negligible.

Additional worked example

If I falls from 6 to 3 kg·m² at initial ω=1 rad/s, find final ω.

ωf=(6/3)(1)=2 rad/s. Rotational kinetic energy rises because the skater does internal work.

Important distinction. Angular momentum can stay constant while rotational kinetic energy changes.

lessons.title: Rigid-body equilibrium
lessons.html:
21

Rigid-body equilibrium

When you see

A beam, sign, or ladder remains at rest.

Choose this model

Rigid object with both translational and rotational equilibrium.

Principle

Zero net force prevents translational acceleration; zero net torque prevents angular acceleration. Both are needed for static equilibrium.

First move

Draw every external force and its application point. Choose a pivot that removes unknown forces from the torque equation.

Worked reasoning

A 20 N downward load 2 m right of a pivot is balanced by a 10 N downward load 4 m left: opposite torque magnitudes are each 40 N·m.

Additional worked example

A 30 N load acts 1 m right of a pivot. What downward load 2 m left balances its torque?

15 N because 30(1)=F(2). Force balance still determines pivot reaction.

Important distinction. Balancing torques alone does not guarantee zero net force.

lessons.title: Elasticity of solids
lessons.html:
22

Elasticity of solids

When you see

A rod stretches slightly under load.

Choose this model

Linear elastic material within its proportional limit.

Principle

Young modulus links tensile stress to strain. The extension grows with force and initial length but falls as area or modulus increases.

First move

Check that deformation is small and reversible; use the original cross-sectional area and length.

Worked reasoning

A 2 m rod with A=1.0×10⁻⁴ m², Y=2.0×10¹¹ Pa, and F=100 N stretches ΔL=FL/(AY)=1.0×10⁻⁵ m.

Additional worked example

Within the elastic range, what happens to extension when force doubles?

Extension doubles. The material and geometry must remain unchanged.

Important distinction. A modulus is a material property; a spring constant also depends on object geometry.

lessons.title: Gravitation and orbital motion
lessons.html:
23

Gravitation and orbital motion

When you see

A body is far from Earth’s surface or moves in an ideal circular orbit.

Choose this model

Two-body gravitational interaction; circular orbit needs inward net force.

Principle

Gravity weakens with center-to-center distance squared. In an ideal circular orbit it supplies the inward force; an orbiting satellite is continuously falling.

First move

Use distance from the attracting body’s center. Match energy reference U=0 at infinite separation, and check whether a circular-orbit assumption is justified.

Worked reasoning

At twice Earth-center distance, gravitational field magnitude is one-quarter as large, ignoring other bodies.

Additional worked example

If circular-orbit radius grows by a factor of 4, how does orbital speed change?

It halves because v scales as 1/sqrt(r) for the same central mass.

Important distinction. Altitude above a surface is not the r in the inverse-square law; add the planet radius.

lessons.title: Pressure and buoyancy
lessons.html:
24

Pressure and buoyancy

When you see

A submerged body or a pressure measurement at depth is given.

Choose this model

Static fluid with pressure increasing downward and upward buoyant resultant.

Principle

Hydrostatic pressure depends on depth, fluid density, and surface pressure, not container shape. Buoyant force equals weight of displaced fluid.

First move

Separate gauge from absolute pressure. For a floating body, balance buoyancy with weight; for sinking or tethering, include all forces.

Worked reasoning

At 5 m depth in water with ρ=1000 kg/m³ and g=10, gauge pressure is 50 kPa. A 0.002 m³ fully displaced volume gives 20 N buoyancy.

Additional worked example

A 1 kg object of volume 0.002 m³ floats in water with g=10. What fraction of its volume is submerged?

Weight is 10 N, so displaced volume is 10/(1000·10)=0.001 m³, half its volume.

Important distinction. Buoyancy uses displaced fluid volume, which equals total object volume only when fully submerged.

lessons.title: Flow and Bernoulli conditions
lessons.html:
25

Flow and Bernoulli conditions

When you see

Fluid moves through a pipe with changing area or height.

Choose this model

Steady incompressible flow; Bernoulli additionally assumes negligible viscous loss along a streamline.

Principle

Continuity is volume-flow conservation for incompressible flow. Bernoulli accounts for pressure, kinetic, and gravitational energy per unit volume under stated conditions.

First move

Solve flow speeds from continuity first. Then compare points on one streamline with consistent height reference.

Worked reasoning

In a horizontal pipe, area halves from 4 to 2 cm² and speed doubles from 1 to 2 m/s. For ideal water, pressure drops by 0.5(1000)(4-1)=1500 Pa.

Additional worked example

A pipe narrows to one-quarter its original area. If initial speed is 0.5 m/s, find new speed for steady incompressible flow.

Speed becomes 2 m/s. The result does not alone determine pressure if elevation or losses are unknown.

Important distinction. Do not use ideal Bernoulli across a pump, substantial frictional loss, or unrelated streamlines without extra terms.

lessons.title: Simple harmonic motion
lessons.html:
26

Simple harmonic motion

When you see

A restoring force is proportional to displacement from stable equilibrium.

Choose this model

Particle in simple harmonic motion; displacement measured from equilibrium.

Principle

Acceleration points toward equilibrium and is largest at the turning points. Speed is greatest at equilibrium, where spring potential energy is least.

First move

Use amplitude A as maximum displacement. Keep ordinary frequency f=1/T distinct from angular frequency ω=2πf.

Worked reasoning

For k=100 N/m, m=1 kg, and A=0.10 m, ω=10 rad/s, T≈0.628 s, and vmax=ωA=1 m/s.

Additional worked example

At the positive turning point of this motion, what are speed and acceleration?

Speed is zero and acceleration is -ω²A=-10 m/s² toward equilibrium.

Important distinction. At a turning point, zero speed does not imply zero acceleration.

lessons.title: Pendulum, damping, and driving
lessons.html:
27

Pendulum, damping, and driving

When you see

A small-angle pendulum swings, or oscillations lose energy or receive periodic driving.

Choose this model

Small-angle oscillator; driving and damping alter amplitude response.

Principle

For small swings, the pendulum period depends mainly on length and g, not bob mass. Damping removes energy; near resonance a drive can transfer energy efficiently.

First move

Check that the angle is small, then compare period using a square-root ratio. For driven motion, distinguish natural frequency from drive frequency.

Worked reasoning

Doubling a small-angle pendulum’s length multiplies its period by sqrt(2), not by 2.

Additional worked example

For L≈1 m and g≈9.8 m/s², estimate the small-angle period.

T≈2πsqrt(1/9.8)≈2.0 s.

Important distinction. The simple pendulum formula is less accurate for large amplitudes.

lessons.title: Traveling waves and sound
lessons.html:
28

Traveling waves and sound

When you see

A disturbance transports energy through a medium.

Choose this model

Traveling-wave model; material points oscillate while the pattern propagates.

Principle

Wave speed is set by medium properties for a given mode of propagation. Frequency comes from the source; wavelength adjusts when speed changes. Sound in air is longitudinal.

First move

Identify frequency, wavelength, and medium. Do not confuse particle speed with the propagation speed of the wave pattern.

Worked reasoning

A string with tension 80 N and linear density 0.20 kg/m has wave speed sqrt(80/0.20)=20 m/s. A 50 Hz wave on it has wavelength 0.40 m.

Additional worked example

A 25 Hz disturbance travels at 10 m/s. Find wavelength.

λ=v/f=0.40 m.

Important distinction. A wave may carry energy while the medium has no net transport along the full path.

lessons.title: Interference and standing waves
lessons.html:
29

Interference and standing waves

When you see

Waves overlap, reflect from a boundary, or resonate in a string or air column.

Choose this model

Superposition of waves with boundary conditions.

Principle

At a node, displacement is always zero; at an antinode, amplitude is largest. Allowed wavelengths are fixed by boundary conditions, not arbitrary harmonic labels.

First move

Sketch nodes and antinodes first. Count half-wavelengths along a string fixed at both ends before choosing n.

Worked reasoning

For a 1 m fixed string with wave speed 100 m/s, fundamental frequency is 50 Hz and second harmonic is 100 Hz.

Additional worked example

What is the third-harmonic frequency of the same string?

150 Hz because f3=3f1. The standing pattern contains three half-wavelengths.

Important distinction. An air column closed at one end has different allowed harmonics; do not import the fixed-string formula unchanged.

lessons.title: Temperature and ideal gas states
lessons.html:
30

Temperature and ideal gas states

When you see

Pressure, volume, or temperature of a dilute gas changes.

Choose this model

Ideal gas in equilibrium; temperature must be absolute.

Principle

The gas law relates equilibrium states of a fixed amount of ideal gas. Pressure at fixed volume and mole number scales with kelvin temperature.

First move

Write two states. Use kelvins and keep n constant only if no gas enters or leaves.

Worked reasoning

Heating a sealed rigid vessel from 300 K to 450 K increases ideal-gas pressure by a factor 450/300=1.5.

Additional worked example

A rigid vessel at 200 kPa and 300 K reaches 600 K. Find final pressure if gas amount stays fixed.

400 kPa because P2/P1=T2/T1=2.

Important distinction. Doubling Celsius temperature does not generally double ideal-gas pressure.

lessons.title: Thermal energy and calorimetry
lessons.html:
31

Thermal energy and calorimetry

When you see

Bodies exchange heat and their temperatures change or a phase transition occurs.

Choose this model

Thermal system; energy transferred by temperature difference.

Principle

Specific heat governs temperature change within one phase. During an ideal phase change at fixed pressure, latent heat changes phase without changing temperature.

First move

Choose the system, set heat lost plus heat gained to zero if insulated, and treat each heating or phase segment separately.

Worked reasoning

Heating 0.50 kg of water by 10 K with c=4200 J/(kg·K) requires Q=0.50·4200·10=21 kJ.

Additional worked example

How much heat is needed to warm 0.20 kg of the same water by 5 K?

Q=0.20·4200·5=4.2 kJ, assuming no phase change or loss.

Important distinction. Use a temperature difference in K or °C, but use kelvins for absolute gas temperatures and entropy formulas.

lessons.title: First law and gas work
lessons.html:
32

First law and gas work

When you see

Heat enters or leaves a gas while its volume may change.

Choose this model

Thermodynamic system with a declared work sign convention.

Principle

Internal energy changes through heat added and work done by the system. Expansion usually gives positive work by the gas; compression gives negative work by the gas.

First move

State whether W means work by or on the gas. On a P-V graph, signed area under the path is work by the gas.

Worked reasoning

A gas receives 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work. Its internal energy rises by 300 J.

Additional worked example

An adiabatic gas is compressed by surroundings doing 150 J of work on it. Find ΔU.

Q=0 and Wby=-150 J, hence ΔU=0-(-150)=+150 J.

Important distinction. For a cyclic process, ΔU=0 over the whole cycle, though heat and work need not each be zero.

lessons.title: Microscopic gas energy
lessons.html:
33

Microscopic gas energy

When you see

The question relates temperature to molecular motion or heat capacity.

Choose this model

Classical monatomic ideal gas, with translational degrees of freedom.

Principle

Absolute temperature measures average molecular translational kinetic energy. Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas depends only on temperature, not separately on pressure or volume.

First move

Check the gas type and model. For a temperature change use ΔU=(3/2)nRΔT.

Worked reasoning

One mole of monatomic ideal gas warmed by 100 K gains about 1.5(8.314)(100)=1.25 kJ of internal energy.

Additional worked example

If two moles of this gas warm by 50 K, what is ΔU?

ΔU=(3/2)(2)(8.314)(50)≈1.25 kJ.

Important distinction. Do not apply the monatomic 3/2 factor to every gas without checking active degrees of freedom.

lessons.title: Heat engines and the Carnot limit
lessons.html:
34

Heat engines and the Carnot limit

When you see

Heat flows between hot and cold reservoirs, sometimes producing work.

Choose this model

Cyclic engine with energy accounting and second-law limit.

Principle

A heat engine cannot turn all intake heat into work while operating cyclically between two reservoirs. Carnot efficiency is the upper limit for reservoir temperatures in kelvins.

First move

Draw heat-input, work-output, and rejected-heat arrows. First use Qh=W+Qc, then compare actual efficiency with the Carnot bound.

Worked reasoning

An engine takes 1000 J and rejects 600 J each cycle. It delivers 400 J and has 40% efficiency. At Th=500 K and Tc=300 K, 40% is the Carnot ceiling.

Additional worked example

If an engine takes 800 J and produces 200 J of work, how much heat does it reject and what is efficiency?

Qc=800-200=600 J and η=200/800=25%.

Important distinction. Carnot efficiency is a maximum under specified reservoir temperatures, not the expected efficiency of every actual engine.

lessons.title: Entropy and refrigeration
lessons.html:
35

Entropy and refrigeration

When you see

Heat flows between reservoirs or a device moves heat from cold to hot.

Choose this model

Thermal system plus surroundings; assess entropy of the combined isolated whole.

Principle

Entropy can decrease in one part while total entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. A refrigerator requires work to extract heat from a cold region and release still more heat to a warm region.

First move

Track positive heat magnitudes and the work input. For a reversible isothermal heat transfer, use ΔS=Qrev/T with kelvin temperature; for an irreversible process, evaluate entropy change along a reversible reference path.

Worked reasoning

A refrigerator removes 300 J from its cold compartment using 100 J of work. It rejects 400 J to the room and has cold-side COP=300/100=3.

Additional worked example

A refrigerator removes 500 J using 200 J of work. Find heat rejected and cold-side COP.

Heat rejected is 700 J by energy balance; COPc=500/200=2.5.

Important distinction. COP can exceed one because it counts heat moved, not work converted into heat; it is not an engine efficiency.
