lessons.title: Units and conversion factors
lessons.html:
01

Units and conversion factors

Meaning

A measured answer needs a number and a unit. A conversion factor is a ratio equal to one, so multiplying by it changes units without changing the physical quantity.

First move

Write the starting unit, multiply by factors that cancel it, and check whether the new numerical size is plausible. Convert to one coherent unit system before substituting into an equation.

Worked reasoning

At 72 km/h, a car travels 72/3.6=20 m/s. In 6 s at constant speed it covers 120 m; the constant-speed condition matters.

Additional worked example

Convert 54 km/h to m/s. How far does it travel in 4 s at that constant speed?

54/3.6=15 m/s; distance=15·4=60 m.

If it went wrong. If the car accelerates, multiplying one reported speed by the full time need not give the distance.

Optional targeted videoIntroduction to Units & the SI System ↗

lessons.title: Significant figures and dimensional checks
lessons.html:
02

Significant figures and dimensional checks

Meaning

Units can reject a wrong equation: terms being added must share dimensions. Report precision supported by measurements, but retain extra digits during intermediate calculations.

First move

Check dimensions before arithmetic. For multiplication or division, use the fewest significant figures in the inputs; for addition or subtraction, use the least precise decimal place.

Worked reasoning

A length 2.0 m divided by 3.00 s is 0.67 m/s to two significant figures. Adding 12.3 m and 0.456 m gives 12.8 m to one decimal place.

Additional worked example

A formula claims distance equals speed plus acceleration times time. Is it dimensionally valid?

No. Both terms on the right have units of speed, not distance.

If it went wrong. Dimensional agreement is necessary but does not prove that the physical model is valid.

lessons.title: Vectors and signed components
lessons.html:
03

Vectors and signed components

Meaning

Direction is part of a vector answer. Components are signed projections on stated axes; the resultant is found by summing components before taking a magnitude.

First move

Draw axes and the vector. Resolve each arrow using the angle measured from the chosen axis; then add x with x and y with y. Use the signs to choose the final quadrant.

Worked reasoning

A 3 N eastward force and a 4 N northward force have components (3,4) N. The resultant is 5 N at 53.1° north of east.

Additional worked example

Combine 6 N west and 8 N north. Give magnitude and direction.

Components are (−6,8) N; magnitude 10 N, at 53.1° north of west.

If it went wrong. Adding 6+8 gives 14 N only for forces along the same line in the same direction.

Optional targeted videoVector Addition By Components ↗

lessons.title: Position, displacement, and speed
lessons.html:
04

Position, displacement, and speed

Meaning

Displacement is the change in position and can be negative or zero. Distance is the length of the path. Average velocity uses displacement; average speed uses distance.

First move

Mark start and finish on an axis. Calculate displacement with signs, and total path length with absolute segment lengths. Divide each by the same elapsed time.

Worked reasoning

A runner goes 40 m east and 10 m west in 10 s. Displacement is 30 m east and distance is 50 m. Average velocity is 3 m/s east; average speed is 5 m/s.

Additional worked example

A walker goes 5 m right, then 5 m left, in 4 s. Find average velocity and average speed.

Displacement is zero, so average velocity is 0; distance is 10 m, so average speed is 2.5 m/s.

If it went wrong. An out-and-back trip can have zero average velocity while motion and nonzero average speed occurred.

lessons.title: Read motion graphs before equations
lessons.html:
05

Read motion graphs before equations

Meaning

A position-time slope gives velocity. A velocity-time slope gives acceleration, while signed area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.

First move

Read both axis labels and units first. For a segment use rise over run. For area split into rectangles or triangles, preserving the sign below the time axis.

Worked reasoning

Velocity rises uniformly from 0 to 6 m/s during 4 s. The triangular area is (1/2)·4·6=12 m of displacement.

Additional worked example

Velocity is −2 m/s for 3 s. Find displacement and distance traveled.

Signed area gives −6 m displacement; distance is 6 m.

If it went wrong. The area under a position-time curve does not generally represent displacement. Use its slope instead.

Optional targeted videoCalculating Displacement from Velocity-Time Graphs ↗

lessons.title: Constant acceleration as a model
lessons.html:
06

Constant acceleration as a model

Meaning

These three relations describe one-dimensional motion only while acceleration is constant over the interval. Signs follow a chosen axis, not the everyday word “slowing.”

First move

Choose positive direction, list known quantities, and choose the relation that omits the unwanted unknown. If motion changes regime, solve one interval at a time.

Worked reasoning

From rest with a=3 m/s² for 4 s, v=12 m/s and displacement=(1/2)·3·16=24 m.

Additional worked example

A cart starts at 5 m/s and accelerates at −1 m/s² for 3 s. Find final velocity and displacement.

v=5−3=2 m/s; displacement=5·3−(1/2)·9=10.5 m.

If it went wrong. Using these equations across a change in acceleration silently assumes one constant value.

Optional targeted videoKinematics Equations ↗

lessons.title: Free fall and the turning point
lessons.html:
07

Free fall and the turning point

Meaning

With upward positive and negligible air drag, free-fall acceleration is −g throughout the flight, including at the highest point where vertical velocity is momentarily zero.

First move

State the launch height and target height. Use v=0 only at the top, not a=0. A return-time symmetry holds only for the same launch and landing height.

Worked reasoning

Thrown upward at 20 m/s with g=10 m/s², a ball reaches its highest point after 2 s and gains 20 m of height.

Additional worked example

A ball is thrown upward at 10 m/s. With g=10 m/s², how long until the top and how high above launch?

At the top 0=10−10t, so t=1 s; height=10·1−5·1²=5 m.

If it went wrong. A zero velocity at one instant does not mean zero acceleration.

lessons.title: Projectile motion in two axes
lessons.html:
08

Projectile motion in two axes

Meaning

In ideal projectile motion, horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is downward. The two axes share the same time, which joins their separate equations.

First move

Resolve launch velocity, solve the vertical equation for the time at the specified target height, and only then use horizontal displacement. Do not assume landing at launch height unless stated.

Worked reasoning

A ball leaves a 20 m ledge horizontally at 8 m/s. With g=10 m/s² it falls for 2 s and lands 16 m horizontally from the ledge.

Additional worked example

From a 45 m ledge, a ball launches horizontally at 6 m/s. With g=10 m/s², find flight time and range.

45=(1/2)·10t² gives t=3 s; range=6·3=18 m.

If it went wrong. The horizontal equation gives no flight time by itself; the height condition provides it.

Optional targeted videoIntroduction to Projectile Motion ↗

lessons.title: Relative velocity and moving frames
lessons.html:
09

Relative velocity and moving frames

Meaning

A velocity value depends on the reference frame. Velocities add as vectors, so opposing motion subtracts through signs rather than through a new rule.

First move

Label each velocity “object relative to reference.” Make the middle reference match before adding, and check direction in the ground frame.

Worked reasoning

A person walks 2 m/s east relative to a train moving 10 m/s east relative to ground. The person moves 12 m/s east relative to ground.

Additional worked example

The person instead walks 2 m/s west relative to the same train. What is the ground-frame velocity?

Take east positive: −2+10=8 m/s east.

If it went wrong. Subtracting speeds without naming reference frames can reverse the answer.

lessons.title: Newton laws and the system boundary
lessons.html:
10

Newton laws and the system boundary

Meaning

Acceleration is caused by the net external force on the chosen object or system. Zero net force means constant velocity, which may be nonzero.

First move

Name the body under study. List only forces acting on that body, pick axes, then write a separate signed force equation for each axis.

Worked reasoning

An 18 N force acts right on a 4 kg cart while 6 N acts left. Net force is 12 N right, so acceleration is 3 m/s² right.

Additional worked example

A 5 kg object has 25 N right and 10 N left. Find acceleration.

Net force 15 N right gives 3 m/s² right.

If it went wrong. The equal-and-opposite reaction force acts on another body, so it does not cancel a force on this body.

Optional targeted videoIntro to Forces & Newton's Second Law ↗

lessons.title: Free-body diagrams and normal force
lessons.html:
11

Free-body diagrams and normal force

Meaning

A free-body diagram is an inventory of real external forces on one isolated body. Weight acts downward; a surface normal acts perpendicular to contact, not always upward.

First move

Replace the body with a dot or box. Draw weight, contact forces, tension, and applied forces from their actual sources. Resolve tilted forces before writing equations.

Worked reasoning

A 5 kg mass hangs at rest from a light string. With g=10 m/s², tension is 50 N because vertical acceleration is zero.

Additional worked example

A 4 kg box rests on a horizontal floor with no other vertical force. What normal force acts, using g=10?

N−mg=0, so N=40 N upward.

If it went wrong. N=mg is a result of this particular vertical balance, not a definition valid for all surfaces.

Optional targeted videoIntro to Forces & Newton's Second Law ↗

lessons.title: Equilibrium with forces in two dimensions
lessons.html:
12

Equilibrium with forces in two dimensions

Meaning

Static equilibrium and constant-velocity motion both require zero acceleration. In two dimensions, horizontal and vertical force components must each balance.

First move

Resolve every angled force, then solve two component equations. Check whether the resulting magnitudes can be drawn in the stated directions.

Worked reasoning

A point has forces 3 N right and 4 N up. A third force of 5 N down-left, with components (−3,−4) N, makes equilibrium.

Additional worked example

For 5 N right and 12 N up, what single force balances them?

A force (−5,−12) N, magnitude 13 N, directed down-left.

If it went wrong. Balancing magnitudes alone misses the direction required by each component equation.

lessons.title: Friction and incline decisions
lessons.html:
13

Friction and incline decisions

Meaning

Static friction supplies only the amount needed up to a maximum. Kinetic friction approximately equals μkN and opposes relative sliding. On an incline, weight splits along and across the plane.

First move

Choose an axis along the plane. Predict actual or impending slip, draw friction opposite it, compute N from the perpendicular balance, then solve along the plane.

Worked reasoning

A 5 kg block slides down a 30° incline with μk=0.20 and g=10. Downhill gravity is 25 N, N≈43.3 N, friction≈8.66 N uphill, and acceleration≈3.27 m/s² downhill.

Additional worked example

A 2 kg block rests on a 30° incline with μs=0.8 and g=10. Is rest possible?

Downhill pull is 10 N; maximum static friction is 0.8·(20 cos30°)≈13.9 N. Rest is possible; actual friction is 10 N uphill.

If it went wrong. Do not automatically set static friction equal to μsN; that is only its limiting value.

Optional targeted videoIntro to Inclined Planes ↗

lessons.title: Tension and connected bodies
lessons.html:
14

Tension and connected bodies

Meaning

A taut massless string over an ideal pulley gives the connected bodies equal acceleration magnitudes. Tension is common only under the ideal-string, ideal-pulley model.

First move

Draw one diagram per mass, choose consistent positive directions along the string, and write both Newton equations before eliminating tension.

Worked reasoning

For hanging masses 2 kg and 3 kg with g=10, acceleration is (3−2)10/5=2 m/s²; the 3 kg mass moves down and the string tension is 24 N.

Additional worked example

For 1 kg and 4 kg masses with g=10, find acceleration and tension.

a=(4−1)10/5=6 m/s². For the 1 kg side, T−10=1·6, so T=16 N.

If it went wrong. The tension is not the heavier weight while the system accelerates.

lessons.title: Springs and elastic force
lessons.html:
15

Springs and elastic force

Meaning

An ideal spring exerts a restoring force proportional to displacement from its unstretched length. The energy stored depends on the square of that displacement.

First move

Mark the equilibrium or unstretched position and the displacement sign. Use the force law for direction and the energy relation for stored work.

Worked reasoning

A spring with k=200 N/m stretched by 0.10 m pulls back with 20 N and stores (1/2)·200·0.10²=1 J.

Additional worked example

For k=100 N/m and stretch 0.20 m, find restoring-force magnitude and stored energy.

Force magnitude is 20 N; energy is (1/2)·100·0.20²=2 J.

If it went wrong. Doubling extension doubles force but quadruples stored energy.

lessons.title: Circular motion and inward force
lessons.html:
16

Circular motion and inward force

Meaning

An object can have constant speed and still accelerate because its velocity direction changes. Centripetal force is the name for the net inward component of real forces.

First move

Draw the circle center, choose inward positive, and identify which real forces have inward components. Use speed at the point of interest, not a force “outward” added to the free-body diagram.

Worked reasoning

At 10 m/s on a radius 5 m circle, centripetal acceleration is 20 m/s². A 2 kg object needs 40 N net inward force.

Additional worked example

A 1 kg object moves at 6 m/s around a 3 m radius. Find net inward force.

F=mv²/r=1·36/3=12 N inward.

If it went wrong. A circular path does not imply an extra physical “centripetal force” in addition to tension, friction, gravity, or the normal force.

Optional targeted videoIntro to Centripetal Forces ↗

lessons.title: Flat and banked curves
lessons.html:
17

Flat and banked curves

Meaning

A flat curve needs static friction to provide inward force. An ideal frictionless bank instead uses the inward component of the normal force.

First move

Draw the force diagram before selecting a formula. The flat-road expression describes the threshold of slip; the bank expression assumes no friction.

Worked reasoning

On a flat curve with μs=0.5, r=20 m, and g=10 m/s², the maximum speed before slipping is √(0.5·20·10)=10 m/s.

Additional worked example

With μs=0.4, r=25 m, and g=10, find the flat-curve speed limit.

vmax=√(0.4·25·10)=10 m/s.

If it went wrong. The two formulas describe different physical assumptions; a banked curve with friction needs a new force balance.

lessons.title: Work by a force
lessons.html:
18

Work by a force

Meaning

Work transfers energy through a force component along displacement. Positive work aids motion, negative work opposes it, and a perpendicular force does zero work.

First move

Mark force and displacement arrows. Use the angle between them, not necessarily the incline angle. For variable force, take signed area under force versus displacement.

Worked reasoning

A 20 N force acts at 60° to a 3 m displacement. Its work is 20·3·cos60°=30 J.

Additional worked example

A 10 N force acts at 120° to a 5 m displacement. Find work.

W=10·5·cos120°=−25 J; this force does negative work.

If it went wrong. Force magnitude times distance misses the sign and the along-path component.

lessons.title: The work-energy checkpoint
lessons.html:
19

The work-energy checkpoint

Meaning

Net work changes kinetic energy. This is useful when the requested speeds and positions matter more than travel time.

First move

Define the initial and final states and include work by every force, with its sign. A constant-speed path has zero net work even if individual forces do work.

Worked reasoning

For a 2 kg body speeding from 3 to 5 m/s, the net work is (1/2)·2·(25−9)=16 J.

Additional worked example

How much net work accelerates a 1 kg body from rest to 6 m/s?

ΔK=(1/2)·1·36=18 J.

If it went wrong. The theorem uses net work, not just the work of one convenient force.

Optional targeted videoThe Work-Energy Theorem ↗

lessons.title: Potential energy and conservation
lessons.html:
20

Potential energy and conservation

Meaning

Gravity and ideal springs can store potential energy. Mechanical energy is conserved only when nonconservative external work is zero for the chosen system.

First move

Choose a height zero and a system boundary. Write initial and final kinetic plus potential energies, then place friction or an applied push as nonconservative work.

Worked reasoning

A 2 kg mass falls 5 m from rest without drag. With g=10, it loses 100 J gravitational potential energy and gains 100 J kinetic energy, reaching 10 m/s.

Additional worked example

A 1 kg object starts at rest 2 m above the ground without drag, with g=10. Find speed at ground.

mgh=(1/2)mv² gives v=√(2gh)=√40≈6.32 m/s.

If it went wrong. Energy conservation without a loss term fails when friction converts mechanical energy to thermal energy.

Optional targeted videoConservation Of Mechanical Energy ↗

lessons.title: Energy losses and thermal transfer
lessons.html:
21

Energy losses and thermal transfer

Meaning

Energy of the larger system remains accounted for, but mechanical energy can decrease when friction or drag converts it to thermal energy.

First move

Compute the change in mechanical energy between states; the missing amount is energy transferred outside the mechanical store. Do not force final speed to match lossless motion.

Worked reasoning

A 2 kg mass falls 5 m from rest and reaches 8 m/s with g=10. It loses 100 J potential energy, gains 64 J kinetic energy, and transfers 36 J to other forms.

Additional worked example

A 1 kg mass drops 2 m from rest and reaches 4 m/s with g=10. How much mechanical energy was dissipated?

Initial potential decrease is 20 J; final kinetic energy is 8 J; dissipated energy is 12 J.

If it went wrong. A negative mechanical-energy change is not missing energy; name the recipient of the transfer.

lessons.title: Power is a rate, not energy
lessons.html:
22

Power is a rate, not energy

Meaning

Power tells how quickly work is done or energy is transferred. One watt is one joule per second; the instantaneous dot-product form uses the along-motion force component.

First move

Decide whether average power over an interval or instantaneous power at one speed is requested. Keep the angle between force and velocity when using Fv.

Worked reasoning

Transferring 600 J in 20 s requires average power 30 W. A 10 N along-motion force at 3 m/s also delivers 30 W instantaneously.

Additional worked example

A machine transfers 900 J in 30 s. Find average power.

P=900/30=30 W.

If it went wrong. Do not label a joule value as watts; divide by time to obtain a rate.

lessons.title: Momentum and system direction
lessons.html:
23

Momentum and system direction

Meaning

Momentum is a vector. The total momentum of a system is a signed or component-wise sum, not the sum of all speed magnitudes.

First move

Choose an axis before multiplying mass and velocity. Add momenta with their signs; in two dimensions, resolve x and y separately.

Worked reasoning

A 2 kg cart moving east at 3 m/s has momentum +6 kg·m/s with east positive.

Additional worked example

A 0.5 kg ball moves west at 4 m/s. Find signed momentum with east positive.

p=0.5·(−4)=−2 kg·m/s, meaning 2 kg·m/s west.

If it went wrong. Kinetic energy cannot substitute for momentum: it is scalar and depends on speed squared.

Optional targeted videoIntro to Momentum ↗

lessons.title: Impulse and force-time area
lessons.html:
24

Impulse and force-time area

Meaning

Impulse is momentum change and equals signed area under a force-time graph. For the same momentum change, longer contact time means smaller average force magnitude.

First move

Find final minus initial momentum with velocity signs. Divide by contact duration only after determining the signed impulse.

Worked reasoning

A 50 N constant force acts for 0.20 s, delivering 10 N·s. A 2 kg object initially at rest gains 5 m/s in the force direction.

Additional worked example

A 0.20 kg ball changes from +15 to −5 m/s in 0.04 s. Find average force.

Δp=0.20(−5−15)=−4 N·s; Favg=−4/0.04=−100 N.

If it went wrong. A rebound reverses velocity direction, so subtracting unsigned speeds understates the momentum change.

Optional targeted videoImpulse & Impulse-Momentum Theorem ↗

lessons.title: Conservation of momentum
lessons.html:
25

Conservation of momentum

Meaning

The momentum of a chosen system stays constant when net external impulse during the event is negligible. Individual objects can change momentum while the system total remains fixed.

First move

Choose all interacting objects as the system, define a positive axis, and write signed initial and final momentum sums. Check whether an external impact invalidates isolation.

Worked reasoning

A 1 kg cart starts at +4 m/s and a 3 kg cart is still. If the first ends at −2 m/s after interaction, the second must move at +2 m/s because 4=−2+3·2.

Additional worked example

A 2 kg cart at +5 m/s hits a 3 kg cart at rest. If the first leaves at −1 m/s, find the second final velocity.

10=−2+3v, so v=4 m/s in the positive direction.

If it went wrong. Momentum conservation does not imply kinetic-energy conservation.

lessons.title: Collisions and energy bookkeeping
lessons.html:
26

Collisions and energy bookkeeping

Meaning

In a completely inelastic collision, bodies stick and share a final velocity. Momentum can be conserved while kinetic energy decreases into deformation, sound, and heat.

First move

Write signed momentum first to obtain shared velocity. Then compare initial and final kinetic energies separately; never assume the latter is conserved.

Worked reasoning

A 1 kg cart at 4 m/s sticks to an identical cart at rest. Final speed is 2 m/s. Initial kinetic energy is 8 J; final kinetic energy is 4 J.

Additional worked example

A 2 kg cart at 3 m/s sticks to a 1 kg cart at rest. Find final speed and kinetic-energy loss.

Momentum gives v=2 m/s. Initial K=9 J and final K=6 J, so 3 J leaves the kinetic store.

If it went wrong. Using an elastic-collision kinetic-energy equation for bodies that stick contradicts the event description.

Optional targeted videoCompletely Inelastic Collisions ↗

lessons.title: Center of mass as a weighted position
lessons.html:
27

Center of mass as a weighted position

Meaning

Center of mass weights each position by its mass. It helps describe the overall motion of a group and lies closer to a larger mass in a two-object system.

First move

Choose one origin and coordinate direction; multiply every mass by its signed position, sum, and divide by total mass.

Worked reasoning

A 1 kg mass at x=0 and 2 kg mass at x=3 m have center of mass x=(0+6)/3=2 m.

Additional worked example

A 2 kg mass is at x=0 and a 1 kg mass at x=6 m. Locate the center of mass.

xcm=(2·0+1·6)/3=2 m, closer to the 2 kg mass.

If it went wrong. A plain average of positions works only when masses are equal.

lessons.title: Calculus connects motion and accumulation
lessons.html:
28

Calculus connects motion and accumulation

Meaning

A derivative gives an instantaneous rate; an integral accumulates signed change. These relations extend the constant-acceleration equations to changing acceleration.

First move

Check the variable and units before differentiating or integrating. State interval endpoints, preserve negative velocity contributions, and include an integration constant when finding a position function.

Worked reasoning

If x(t)=2t²+3t metres, then v(t)=4t+3 m/s and a(t)=4 m/s². At t=2 s, velocity is 11 m/s.

Additional worked example

If v(t)=3t² m/s, find displacement from t=0 to 2 s.

The integral is [t³] from 0 to 2, giving 8 m.

If it went wrong. Integrating speed instead of signed velocity gives distance, which differs when direction reverses.

lessons.title: Measurements, units, and model limits
lessons.html:
01

Measurements, units, and model limits

Physical idea

A number is a physical answer only when its units and meaning are clear. Dimensional analysis checks whether an equation can be sensible; it cannot prove that the physics model is correct.

First move

Before calculating, identify the system, draw a simple representation, convert to SI units, and state the approximation. Compare dimensions on both sides of an equation and round the final result to a precision justified by the data.

Worked reasoning

A car moves at 72 km/h. Dividing by 3.6 gives 20 m/s. In 5 s at constant speed it travels 100 m. The calculation would fail if the car were accelerating and 72 km/h were only its starting speed.

Additional worked example

A runner covers 150 m in 25 s. Find average speed and check its units.

150/25 = 6.0 m/s. Distance divided by time has dimension L/T.

Common error. A mathematically consistent result can still use the wrong model; write the condition that makes the equation valid.

lessons.title: Vectors, components, and direction
lessons.html:
02

Vectors, components, and direction

Physical idea

Scalars have magnitude; vectors also have direction. Components are signed projections on chosen axes. Vector addition operates component by component, not by adding magnitudes unless the vectors are collinear and aligned.

First move

Draw axes and an arrow. Resolve every vector into x and y components using an angle measured from the stated axis. Add components, then find magnitude and quadrant of the resultant. Keep signs attached to components.

Worked reasoning

A 10 N force at 30° above +x has components (8.66, 5.00) N. Added to a 4 N downward force, it gives (8.66, 1.00) N, with magnitude about 8.72 N.

Additional worked example

Add 3 m east and 4 m north. State magnitude and direction north of east.

The displacement is (3,4) m, magnitude 5 m, at arctan(4/3) ≈ 53.1° north of east.

Common error. An angle found from arctan(Ay/Ax) needs a quadrant check when either component is negative.

lessons.title: Position, velocity, acceleration, and motion graphs
lessons.html:
03

Position, velocity, acceleration, and motion graphs

Physical idea

Displacement is final minus initial position and can be negative. Speed uses distance traveled; velocity uses displacement. On a position-time graph slope is velocity. On a velocity-time graph slope is acceleration and signed area is displacement.

First move

Read axis labels first. For a straight segment, calculate rise over run. For area under v(t), split the region into familiar shapes and preserve area below the time axis as negative.

Worked reasoning

Velocity rises linearly from 0 to 8 m/s in 4 s, then stays at 8 m/s for 2 s. Displacement is triangle 16 m plus rectangle 16 m, totaling 32 m.

Additional worked example

A body moves at +3 m/s for 4 s, then −2 m/s for 3 s. Find displacement and total distance.

Displacement is 12−6=6 m. Distance is 12+6=18 m.

Common error. Area under a velocity graph is displacement, not always distance; use absolute areas for distance.

lessons.title: Constant acceleration and free fall
lessons.html:
04

Constant acceleration and free fall

Physical idea

These kinematic relations apply to constant acceleration along one axis. For near-Earth free fall without appreciable air drag, vertical acceleration is approximately −g if up is positive, even while the object rises.

First move

Choose a positive direction, list known and unknown quantities, and select the relation that excludes the variable you do not have. Check whether the acceleration is constant before using these equations.

Worked reasoning

A ball is thrown upward at 20 m/s with g≈10 m/s². At the top v=0, so 0=20−10t and t=2 s. Its rise is 20(2)−5(2²)=20 m.

Additional worked example

A car starts at 5 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. Find final speed and displacement.

v=5+2(4)=13 m/s; Δx=5(4)+0.5(2)(4²)=36 m.

Common error. At the top of a vertical throw velocity is zero for an instant; acceleration is still downward.

lessons.title: Projectile and relative motion
lessons.html:
05

Projectile and relative motion

Physical idea

Ideal projectile motion has constant horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration due to gravity. The two components share time but otherwise solve independently. Relative velocity depends on the chosen reference frame.

First move

Resolve launch velocity, solve the vertical equation for flight time at the specified height, then insert that time in the horizontal equation. For relative motion, subtract the observer velocity vector.

Worked reasoning

From a level surface, launch at 20 m/s and 30° with g≈10 m/s². The vertical component is 10 m/s, so the return time is 2 s. Horizontal component is 17.3 m/s, giving range about 34.6 m.

Additional worked example

A boat moves east at 5 m/s relative to water while the river flows north at 2 m/s. Find its speed relative to shore.

The shore-frame velocity is (5,2) m/s and speed is √29≈5.39 m/s. Its path points north of east.

Common error. The familiar level-ground range formula fails when launch and landing heights differ.

lessons.title: Newton laws and free body diagrams
lessons.html:
06

Newton laws and free body diagrams

Physical idea

An object accelerates when the vector sum of external forces is nonzero. A free body diagram contains forces acting on one chosen object. Newton third-law partners act on different objects and cannot cancel on one diagram.

First move

Isolate the body, draw only real external forces, choose axes, and write a force equation for each axis. If acceleration is zero, the sum is zero; a moving object can still have zero acceleration.

Worked reasoning

A 2 kg block on a horizontal frictionless surface is pulled right by 6 N. Its weight and normal force cancel vertically, while horizontal acceleration is 6/2=3 m/s².

Additional worked example

A 4 kg object has 18 N right and 6 N left. Find its acceleration.

Net force is 12 N right, so a=12/4=3 m/s² right.

Common error. Do not put the force exerted by the object on its surroundings on the object’s own free body diagram.

lessons.title: Friction and inclined planes
lessons.html:
07

Friction and inclined planes

Physical idea

Static friction adjusts up to a maximum. Kinetic friction has approximate magnitude μkN and opposes slipping. On a plane inclined at angle θ, gravity has a downhill component mg sinθ and a perpendicular component mg cosθ.

First move

Choose one axis along the plane. Determine the direction of actual or impending relative motion before drawing friction. Compute N from the perpendicular force balance if the object has no perpendicular acceleration.

Worked reasoning

A 5 kg block slides down a 30° incline with μk=0.20 and g=10 m/s². Downhill gravity is 25 N; N≈43.3 N and friction≈8.66 N uphill. Acceleration is (25−8.66)/5≈3.27 m/s² downhill.

Additional worked example

A 2 kg block is at rest on a 30° incline with μs=0.8 and g=10. Is rest possible?

Downhill force is 10 N; N≈17.3 N, so maximum static friction≈13.9 N. Rest is possible and actual friction is 10 N uphill.

Common error. Static friction is not automatically μsN; that expression is only its limiting value.

lessons.title: Connected objects and tension
lessons.html:
08

Connected objects and tension

Physical idea

Objects joined by a taut, light string over an ideal pulley share the same acceleration magnitude. The string tension is the same on both sides only under the ideal string and pulley model.

First move

Draw a separate free body diagram for each mass. Pick one consistent positive direction along the string for the whole system. Write both force equations, then eliminate tension to solve acceleration.

Worked reasoning

For m1=2 kg and m2=3 kg, with g=10, the ideal Atwood acceleration is (3−2)10/5=2 m/s², with m2 downward. From T−m1g=m1a, tension is 24 N.

Additional worked example

For 1 kg and 3 kg masses on an ideal pulley, find acceleration using g=10.

a=(3−1)10/(1+3)=5 m/s²; the 3 kg mass moves down.

Common error. Do not set tension equal to the heavier weight when the system accelerates.

lessons.title: Impulse and momentum
lessons.html:
09

Impulse and momentum

Physical idea

Momentum is a vector. Impulse is the change in momentum and equals the signed area under a force-time graph. Extending stopping time reduces average force for a fixed momentum change.

First move

Choose a direction and calculate final momentum minus initial momentum. For variable force, use graph area or an integral. Average force is Δp/Δt over the same interval.

Worked reasoning

A 0.15 kg ball approaches at +20 m/s and rebounds at −10 m/s. Its momentum change is 0.15(−10−20)=−4.5 N·s. If contact lasts 0.03 s, average force on the ball is −150 N.

Additional worked example

A 2 kg cart slows from +5 to +1 m/s in 0.5 s. Find impulse and average force.

Δp=2(1−5)=−8 N·s; Favg=−8/0.5=−16 N.

Common error. For a rebound, the velocity sign changes. Subtracting speed magnitudes loses that direction change.

lessons.title: Collisions and system boundaries
lessons.html:
10

Collisions and system boundaries

Physical idea

Momentum is conserved for an isolated system during a collision. Kinetic energy is conserved only for an elastic collision. Objects that stick together share one final velocity.

First move

Define both bodies as the system and mark velocity directions. Write momentum conservation first. Add kinetic-energy conservation only when the collision is stated or shown to be elastic.

Worked reasoning

A 2 kg cart at +3 m/s sticks to a 1 kg cart initially at rest. Final speed is (2·3)/(2+1)=2 m/s. Kinetic energy drops from 9 J to 6 J, so the collision is inelastic.

Additional worked example

A 1 kg cart at +4 m/s sticks to a 3 kg cart at rest. Find final velocity.

Total momentum is +4 kg·m/s and total mass is 4 kg, so vf=+1 m/s.

Common error. Mechanical energy need not remain mechanical in an inelastic collision, although total energy remains conserved.

lessons.title: Circular motion and inward force
lessons.html:
11

Circular motion and inward force

Physical idea

Constant speed around a circle still means acceleration because velocity direction changes. The net radial force points toward the center; centripetal force is a role played by real forces, not an extra force to draw.

First move

Choose inward as positive and name the real forces with radial components. Write their signed radial sum as mv²/r. Use tangential equations separately if speed changes.

Worked reasoning

A 2 kg mass moves at 3 m/s in a circle of radius 1.5 m. Required inward net force is 2·9/1.5=12 N. If a string supplies it, tension is 12 N only when other radial forces are absent.

Additional worked example

A 1 kg object moves at 6 m/s around a 2 m circle. Find inward acceleration and net radial force.

ac=36/2=18 m/s² and Fr=1·18=18 N inward.

Common error. Do not add a separate “centripetal force” arrow to real tension, gravity, or friction arrows.

lessons.title: Gravity and circular orbits
lessons.html:
12

Gravity and circular orbits

Physical idea

Gravity acts between masses at center-to-center separation r. In a circular orbit, gravity itself provides the inward acceleration. Orbital speed depends on central mass and orbital radius in the ideal two-body approximation.

First move

Use distance from the central body’s center, not altitude alone. For an orbit, equate GMm/r² to mv²/r. Check that the object is in a circular orbit before using the speed result.

Worked reasoning

If orbit radius doubles around the same planet, the gravitational force falls to one quarter and circular orbital speed falls by a factor of 1/√2.

Additional worked example

At what factor does gravitational force change if separation triples?

It becomes 1/9 of its original magnitude, since force varies as 1/r².

Common error. Doubling altitude does not necessarily double orbital radius; add the planet’s radius first.

lessons.title: Angular motion and torque
lessons.html:
13

Angular motion and torque

Physical idea

Angular displacement and angular speed describe how a rigid body turns. Torque measures how strongly a force tends to rotate it, depending on force magnitude, lever arm, and the angle between them.

First move

Use radians in v=rω. For torque, measure r from the chosen pivot to the point where force acts, then use only the component perpendicular to r. Assign positive or negative torque by rotation sense.

Worked reasoning

A 10 N force perpendicular to a 0.30 m wrench produces torque 3.0 N·m. If the same force acts along the wrench, sinφ=0 and torque about the bolt is zero.

Additional worked example

A wheel has radius 0.20 m and angular speed 15 rad/s. Find rim speed.

v=rω=0.20·15=3.0 m/s.

Common error. Force alone does not determine torque; the perpendicular lever arm matters.

lessons.title: Rotational dynamics and angular momentum
lessons.html:
14

Rotational dynamics and angular momentum

Physical idea

Moment of inertia measures resistance to angular acceleration and depends on mass distribution about a specified axis. With negligible external torque, angular momentum is conserved even if rotational kinetic energy changes.

First move

State the axis, use its correct I, and include all external torques. For conservation questions, compare initial and final Iω; a smaller I requires a larger ω when L stays constant.

Worked reasoning

A rotating system reduces I from 4 to 2 kg·m² while no external torque acts. If ω initially is 3 rad/s, final ω is (4·3)/2=6 rad/s. Rotational energy rises because internal work was done.

Additional worked example

A wheel with I=0.5 kg·m² experiences net torque 2 N·m. Find angular acceleration.

α=τ/I=2/0.5=4 rad/s².

Common error. Do not treat I as simply total mass; geometry and the chosen rotation axis change it.

lessons.title: Work, energy, and power
lessons.html:
15

Work, energy, and power

Physical idea

Work transfers energy when a force acts through displacement. Only the force component along motion contributes work. Power measures the rate of energy transfer, not the amount of energy itself.

First move

Identify the force and displacement direction. For a constant force use W=Fd cosθ. Compare net work with change in kinetic energy and keep joules and watts distinct.

Worked reasoning

A 20 N force acts 3 m at 60° to motion. Work is 20·3·cos60°=30 J. If that work occurs in 2 s, average power is 15 W.

Additional worked example

A 4 kg object speeds up from 2 to 4 m/s. Find net work.

ΔK=0.5·4·(4²−2²)=24 J.

Common error. A force perpendicular to displacement can change direction without doing work.

lessons.title: Conservation of energy and losses
lessons.html:
16

Conservation of energy and losses

Physical idea

Total energy is conserved. Mechanical energy K+U remains constant only when nonconservative work is zero. Gravitational U near Earth is mgh; spring energy is ½kx² relative to the unstretched state.

First move

Choose system and reference height. Mark starting and ending states, then list stored energies and external or dissipative work. If friction acts, its work is typically negative on mechanical energy.

Worked reasoning

A 2 kg object drops 5 m with g=10 and no drag. It loses 100 J of gravitational energy and gains 100 J of kinetic energy. If 20 J is dissipated, final kinetic energy is 80 J.

Additional worked example

A 1 kg object starts from rest 3 m above a reference level. With g=10 and no losses, find speed at the reference level.

mgh=½mv² gives v=√(2gh)=√60≈7.75 m/s.

Common error. “Energy conserved” never means kinetic energy alone is conserved.

lessons.title: Springs and simple harmonic motion
lessons.html:
17

Springs and simple harmonic motion

Physical idea

A spring force points toward equilibrium and grows with displacement. In ideal simple harmonic motion, energy alternates between kinetic and spring potential while total mechanical energy stays fixed.

First move

Measure x from equilibrium and keep the restoring-force sign. Use T=2π√(m/k) only for an ideal mass-spring system. At endpoints speed is zero; at equilibrium speed is greatest.

Worked reasoning

For m=1 kg and k=100 N/m, T=2π/10≈0.628 s. If amplitude is 0.20 m, total oscillation energy is ½·100·0.20²=2 J.

Additional worked example

If spring stiffness quadruples while mass stays fixed, how does period change?

T is proportional to 1/√k, so period is halved.

Common error. The object’s acceleration is largest in magnitude at the endpoints, not at equilibrium.

lessons.title: Density, pressure, and buoyancy
lessons.html:
18

Density, pressure, and buoyancy

Physical idea

Pressure is normal force per area. A fluid pushes harder at greater depth, and a submerged object experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of displaced fluid. Floating equilibrium requires buoyant force to equal the object’s weight.

First move

For buoyancy, use the displaced fluid’s density and displaced volume, not automatically the object’s full volume. Compare buoyant force with weight before deciding whether an object rises, sinks, or floats.

Worked reasoning

A fully submerged 0.002 m³ object in water with ρ=1000 kg/m³ and g=10 receives Fb=20 N. If it weighs 15 N, the net force is 5 N upward before drag.

Additional worked example

A 3 kg object displaces 0.002 m³ of water while fully submerged. With g=10, find its initial net vertical force.

Weight is 30 N down; buoyancy is 20 N up; net force is 10 N down.

Common error. Buoyancy uses fluid density, while the object’s weight uses object mass.

lessons.title: Fluid flow and Bernoulli reasoning
lessons.html:
19

Fluid flow and Bernoulli reasoning

Physical idea

For steady incompressible flow through a pipe, a narrower section has greater speed. Bernoulli’s equation relates pressure, speed, and height along a streamline when viscosity and pump losses are negligible.

First move

Check the flow assumptions first. Apply continuity to obtain speed, then Bernoulli along the same streamline. At the same height, increased speed corresponds to lower static pressure in this ideal model.

Worked reasoning

A pipe narrows from 4 cm² to 2 cm² while flow speed is 1 m/s upstream. Continuity gives 2 m/s downstream. At equal height, ideal pressure falls by ½ρ(2²−1²).

Additional worked example

An ideal horizontal pipe halves its cross-sectional area. What happens to speed?

It doubles because Av stays constant for steady incompressible flow.

Common error. Do not claim fast flow always means low pressure outside the assumptions and streamline comparison of Bernoulli’s equation.

lessons.title: Temperature, heat, phase change, and expansion
lessons.html:
20

Temperature, heat, phase change, and expansion

Physical idea

Temperature measures thermal state; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Sensible heating changes temperature. A phase change can absorb or release energy at nearly constant temperature.

First move

Separate each segment of a heating process: use mcΔT within a phase, mL at a phase boundary, and sum the energy transfers. For thermal expansion use the material’s expansion coefficient and original length.

Worked reasoning

Heating 0.5 kg of water by 10°C with c≈4200 J/(kg·°C) takes 0.5·4200·10=21,000 J, ignoring losses. Melting ice instead requires latent heat and cannot use this temperature-change step alone.

Additional worked example

How much heat raises 2 kg of material with c=500 J/(kg·°C) by 3°C?

Q=2·500·3=3000 J.

Common error. Do not use ΔT in °C as an absolute gas-law temperature; use kelvin there.

lessons.title: Ideal gases and molecular motion
lessons.html:
21

Ideal gases and molecular motion

Physical idea

The ideal gas law links pressure, volume, amount of gas, and absolute temperature. Its particle model works best when interactions and molecular volume are small relative to the container and mean separation.

First move

Convert temperature to kelvin. Keep n fixed only if gas does not enter or leave. For a two-state problem divide PV=nRT at each state to cancel constants that truly remain fixed.

Worked reasoning

A sealed rigid container warms from 300 K to 450 K. Since n and V are fixed, pressure rises by factor 450/300=1.5, not by the ratio of Celsius readings.

Additional worked example

A fixed amount of ideal gas at constant pressure warms from 200 K to 300 K. How does volume change?

Volume becomes 300/200=1.5 times its initial value.

Common error. A temperature ratio is meaningful in kelvin, not Celsius.

lessons.title: First law and thermal processes
lessons.html:
22

First law and thermal processes

Physical idea

The first law tracks internal energy: heat into the system raises U, while work done by the system lowers it. In a pressure-volume graph, signed area under the path is work by the gas.

First move

Declare the sign convention. For a constant-volume process, Wby=0. For an isothermal ideal-gas process, ΔU=0. For an adiabatic process, Q=0. Use the path to find work; endpoints alone are insufficient.

Worked reasoning

A gas receives 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. Its internal energy increases by 300 J. If the same 200 J work were done on the gas, the sign of Wby would reverse.

Additional worked example

A gas loses 100 J of heat and 40 J of work is done on it. Find ΔU.

Q=−100 J and Wby=−40 J, so ΔU=−100−(−40)=−60 J.

Common error. Thermal energy moves as heat because of temperature difference; work and heat are transfers, not stored substances.

lessons.title: Charge, Coulomb force, and electric field
lessons.html:
23

Charge, Coulomb force, and electric field

Physical idea

Charge is conserved. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. An electric field is force per unit positive test charge, so its direction is defined independently of the sign of a charge later placed in it.

First move

Draw charges and displacement vectors. Add electric fields as vectors, then multiply the net field by the actual test charge to get force. Use the inverse-square distance between charge centers.

Worked reasoning

A +2 μC charge in a rightward field of 300 N/C experiences 6×10⁻⁴ N right. A −2 μC charge in the same field feels the same magnitude left.

Additional worked example

A −3 μC charge sits in a field of 200 N/C pointing east. Find force magnitude and direction.

Magnitude is 3×10⁻⁶·200=6×10⁻⁴ N, directed west.

Common error. Field direction follows the force on a positive test charge; a negative charge moves oppositely under electric force alone.

lessons.title: Electric potential and energy
lessons.html:
24

Electric potential and energy

Physical idea

Electric potential is energy per unit charge and is a scalar. Potential difference determines the change in electric potential energy of a charge. A negative charge reverses the sign of ΔU for a given ΔV.

First move

Keep voltage and energy distinct. Add potentials algebraically from multiple point charges, but add fields vectorially. Use energy conservation to connect electric potential change with kinetic change when no other work occurs.

Worked reasoning

A +2 μC charge moves through a +5 V potential change. ΔU=qΔV=+10 μJ, so its kinetic energy decreases by 10 μJ if electric force is the only force doing work.

Additional worked example

A −1 μC charge moves from 10 V to 4 V. Find ΔU.

ΔV=−6 V, so ΔU=(−1 μC)(−6 V)=+6 μJ.

Common error. Higher electric potential does not always mean higher potential energy for a negative charge.

lessons.title: Current, resistance, and electrical power
lessons.html:
25

Current, resistance, and electrical power

Physical idea

Current is charge flow rate. Resistance links voltage and current for an ohmic element under fixed conditions. Electrical power measures energy transfer per time; a resistor generally converts electrical energy to thermal energy.

First move

Use conventional current direction consistently. Determine whether voltage, current, or resistance is fixed before predicting power changes. Convert mA, kΩ, and hours to SI units before calculating energy.

Worked reasoning

A 6 Ω resistor across 12 V carries 2 A and dissipates P=12·2=24 W. In 10 s it transfers 240 J of energy.

Additional worked example

A 4 Ω resistor carries 3 A. Find voltage and power.

V=IR=12 V and P=I²R=36 W.

Common error. Increasing resistance lowers power at fixed voltage but raises power at fixed current.

lessons.title: Series and parallel circuit decisions
lessons.html:
26

Series and parallel circuit decisions

Physical idea

Series elements share current; parallel branches share potential difference. Junction current is conserved, and voltage changes around a closed loop sum to zero.

First move

Mark nodes and branches first. Collapse unmistakable series or parallel groups, then use V=IR. When a connection is not reducible, write Kirchhoff junction and loop equations instead of forcing a series-parallel label.

Worked reasoning

Two resistors 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series across 20 V have equivalent 10 Ω, current 2 A, and drops 8 V and 12 V. In parallel across 20 V, each sees 20 V and their currents differ.

Additional worked example

Two 6 Ω resistors are connected in parallel across 12 V. Find equivalent resistance and total current.

Rp=3 Ω and Itotal=12/3=4 A; each branch carries 2 A.

Common error. An ideal ammeter goes in series and has negligible resistance; an ideal voltmeter goes in parallel and has very high resistance.

lessons.title: Capacitors and RC transients
lessons.html:
27

Capacitors and RC transients

Physical idea

A capacitor stores separated charge and energy. For an RC circuit, the time constant sets the pace of exponential charging or discharging. After one time constant, charging has reached about 63% of its final voltage and discharging retains about 37%.

First move

Find equivalent capacitance with the rule opposite to resistance: parallel capacitances add; reciprocal values add in series. For a DC steady state, an ideal capacitor branch carries no current.

Worked reasoning

With R=2 kΩ and C=100 μF, τ=RC=0.20 s. Charging toward 10 V gives about 6.3 V across the capacitor after 0.20 s.

Additional worked example

Two capacitors, 2 μF and 3 μF, are in parallel. Find equivalent capacitance and charge at 10 V.

Ceq=5 μF; Q=CeqV=50 μC.

Common error. Do not apply the resistance series rule to capacitors; the combinations reverse.

lessons.title: Magnetic force on charges and wires
lessons.html:
28

Magnetic force on charges and wires

Physical idea

A magnetic field acts on moving charge or current perpendicular to both motion and field. Magnetic force on a single particle changes direction of motion but does no work because it is perpendicular to velocity.

First move

Use a right-hand rule for positive charge or conventional current; reverse force for negative charge. Apply the sine factor for the angle between velocity or wire and field.

Worked reasoning

A +1 μC charge moves at 1000 m/s perpendicular to a 0.5 T field. Force magnitude is 1×10⁻⁶·1000·0.5=5×10⁻⁴ N.

Additional worked example

A 0.20 m wire carries 3 A perpendicular to a 0.4 T field. Find force magnitude.

F=ILB=3·0.20·0.4=0.24 N.

Common error. A stationary electric charge feels no magnetic force from a static magnetic field.

lessons.title: Magnetic flux and induction
lessons.html:
29

Magnetic flux and induction

Physical idea

Changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an emf. The induced current, if a closed path exists, produces a field opposing the change in flux, not necessarily the original field itself.

First move

Define the surface normal to interpret angle φ. Compare initial and final flux, then divide by elapsed time and multiply by turns. Use Lenz’s law to determine direction only after identifying whether the flux is increasing or decreasing.

Worked reasoning

Flux through a 10-turn coil increases from 0.01 to 0.03 Wb per turn in 0.2 s. Induced emf magnitude is 10(0.02/0.2)=1 V.

Additional worked example

A 20-turn coil has flux per turn fall by 0.005 Wb in 0.1 s. Find emf magnitude.

|emf|=20·0.005/0.1=1 V.

Common error. A changing field is not the only way to change flux; changing area or orientation also works.

lessons.title: Wave speed, frequency, and energy transport
lessons.html:
30

Wave speed, frequency, and energy transport

Physical idea

A wave transfers energy and disturbance without transporting the medium as a whole over the same distance. Frequency is set by the source; wavelength adjusts when speed changes in a new medium.

First move

Identify what oscillates and what travels. Use v=fλ with consistent units. Read amplitude as maximum displacement, wavelength as spatial repeat distance, and period as time for one cycle.

Worked reasoning

A wave with frequency 50 Hz travels at 200 m/s. Its wavelength is 200/50=4 m, and period is 1/50=0.02 s.

Additional worked example

A wave has wavelength 0.5 m and frequency 8 Hz. Find speed.

v=fλ=8·0.5=4 m/s.

Common error. When a wave enters a new medium, its source frequency usually stays fixed while speed and wavelength change.

lessons.title: Superposition and standing waves
lessons.html:
31

Superposition and standing waves

Physical idea

When waves overlap, displacements add. Interference can be constructive or destructive. A standing wave forms from oppositely traveling waves and has stationary nodes and antinodes.

First move

For a string fixed at both ends, put nodes at endpoints, fit n half-wavelengths in length L, and use f=v/λ. Check boundary conditions; a tube closed at one end has a different harmonic series.

Worked reasoning

A 1 m string has wave speed 100 m/s. Its fundamental wavelength is 2L=2 m, so f1=50 Hz. The next allowed frequency is 100 Hz.

Additional worked example

For the same string, find the third harmonic wavelength.

λ3=2L/3=2/3 m.

Common error. Do not use the fixed-string harmonic rule for a tube closed at one end, where only odd harmonics occur in the ideal model.

lessons.title: Sound, Doppler shift, and wave behavior
lessons.html:
32

Sound, Doppler shift, and wave behavior

Physical idea

Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave and needs a medium. Relative motion between source and observer changes the frequency received. Reflection, diffraction, and interference depend on wavelength and geometry.

First move

For Doppler questions, first predict whether pitch should rise or fall. Then choose source and observer signs so approaching motion raises the calculated frequency. State that the displayed relation assumes speeds along the line of sight in still air.

Worked reasoning

A stationary source emits 500 Hz and an observer moves toward it at 10 m/s in air where v=340 m/s. Received frequency is 500(350/340)≈515 Hz.

Additional worked example

If a sound source approaches a stationary observer, should received frequency be above or below emitted frequency?

Above; wavefronts are compressed in front of the approaching source.

Common error. Do not use this sound-in-medium equation for light in vacuum.

lessons.title: Reflection, mirrors, and image signs
lessons.html:
33

Reflection, mirrors, and image signs

Physical idea

Reflection obeys equal incident and reflected angles measured from the normal. The thin mirror equation links focal length, object distance, and image distance. Magnification sign distinguishes upright from inverted images under a consistent convention.

First move

Sketch the mirror, principal axis, focal point, and object. Apply a stated sign convention; a concave mirror has positive f in the common real-is-positive convention. Check a numerical answer against a simple ray sketch.

Worked reasoning

For a concave mirror with f=10 cm and object at 30 cm, 1/di=1/10−1/30=1/15, so di=15 cm. Magnification is −15/30=−0.5: a smaller inverted real image.

Additional worked example

A plane mirror has an object 2 m in front. Where is its image?

2 m behind the mirror, upright and the same size; it is virtual.

Common error. The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface.

lessons.title: Refraction, lenses, and total internal reflection
lessons.html:
34

Refraction, lenses, and total internal reflection

Physical idea

Light changes speed and wavelength when crossing media, while frequency stays fixed. Snell’s law relates angles measured from the normal. A converging lens may make a real or virtual image depending on object position.

First move

Draw the normal and decide whether the ray bends toward it (higher refractive index) or away from it (lower index). For a lens, sketch principal rays before using the thin-lens equation and sign convention.

Worked reasoning

Light travels from n1=1 to n2=1.5 at 30° to the normal. sinθ2=(1/1.5)sin30°=1/3, so θ2≈19.5°, toward the normal.

Additional worked example

For light going from glass n=1.5 to air n=1, can total internal reflection occur?

Yes, above critical angle θc=arcsin(1/1.5)≈41.8°. It cannot occur in the reverse direction.

Common error. Total internal reflection requires travel from higher to lower refractive index and a sufficiently large incidence angle.

lessons.title: Interference, diffraction, and wave nature of light
lessons.html:
35

Interference, diffraction, and wave nature of light

Physical idea

Coherent light waves can reinforce or cancel. A double-slit bright fringe occurs when path difference is an integer number of wavelengths. Diffraction spreads a wave after an opening or edge, especially when its size is comparable to wavelength.

First move

Identify whether the setup is double-slit interference or single-aperture diffraction before choosing a condition. Keep slit separation d distinct from screen distance; small-angle geometry may be needed to convert angle to screen position.

Worked reasoning

For d=0.50 mm and λ=500 nm, first bright fringe satisfies sinθ=λ/d=0.001, so θ≈0.001 rad. Reducing d spreads the interference fringes farther apart.

Additional worked example

If wavelength increases while slit separation stays fixed, how does fringe spacing change?

It increases because the bright-fringe angle scales approximately with λ/d for small angles.

Common error. A diffraction minimum uses a different condition from a double-slit interference maximum.

lessons.title: Photons, atomic energy, and wave particle reasoning
lessons.html:
36

Photons, atomic energy, and wave particle reasoning

Physical idea

Light has wave behavior but exchanges energy in photons. Electrons and other matter also have wavelengths. Discrete atomic energy levels produce or absorb photons whose energy equals the level difference.

First move

In a transition, compute |ΔE| and set it equal to hf. Emission moves to a lower energy state; absorption moves upward. For a particle wavelength use momentum p, not its kinetic energy directly.

Worked reasoning

A photon with frequency 6×10¹⁴ Hz has energy about (6.63×10⁻³⁴)(6×10¹⁴)=4.0×10⁻¹⁹ J. An atom emitting that photon loses the same energy.

Additional worked example

If photon wavelength doubles, what happens to its energy?

It halves because E=hc/λ.

Common error. Greater light intensity adds photons; it does not raise the energy of each photon if frequency is unchanged.

lessons.title: Nuclear reactions, decay, and mass energy
lessons.html:
37

Nuclear reactions, decay, and mass energy

Physical idea

Nuclear identity follows proton number; isotopes differ in neutron count. Radioactive half-life describes the fraction of undecayed nuclei remaining. Mass differences in nuclear reactions correspond to large energy transfers.

First move

Balance mass number and charge number across a nuclear reaction. Count elapsed half-lives rather than subtracting a fixed number of nuclei. Distinguish alpha, beta, and gamma changes.

Worked reasoning

After three half-lives, an initial 80 g radioactive sample has 80·(1/2)³=10 g of that undecayed isotope. Daughter products account for the rest, ignoring other losses.

Additional worked example

A sample has 32 mg of an isotope and half-life 5 days. How much remains after 15 days?

Three half-lives pass, so 32/8=4 mg remains undecayed.

Common error. Half-life is a fixed time for halving, not a fixed amount lost each interval.

lessons.title: Classify the sample
lessons.html:
Classify the sample

Principle. A pure substance has a fixed chemical identity. An element contains one atomic kind; a compound contains fixed ratios of elements. A mixture is a physical combination and may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

Decision. Ask whether composition can vary and whether separation changes chemical identity.

Worked case. Air is a homogeneous mixture; liquid water is a compound.

Remember. A uniform appearance does not prove a pure substance.

lessons.title: Measure with honest precision
lessons.html:
Measure with honest precision

Principle. Measured digits include one estimated digit. Accuracy means closeness to the accepted value; precision means repeatability. Report a result to the precision justified by the least precise measurement.

Decision. For products or quotients, keep the fewest significant figures. For sums or differences, keep the fewest decimal places.

Worked case. 2.4 cm × 3.15 cm = 7.6 cm²; 2.4 + 3.15 = 5.6 cm.

Remember. Do not round intermediate values early.

lessons.title: Convert units as a chain
lessons.html:
Convert units as a chain

Principle. Multiply by conversion factors equal to one; cancel units before calculating. Density links mass and volume.

Decision. If the requested unit does not remain after cancellation, the factor is inverted.

Worked case. 25.0 mL × (1 L / 1000 mL) = 0.0250 L.

Remember. Temperature for gas laws must be in kelvin.

lessons.title: Identify atoms and ions
lessons.html:
Identify atoms and ions

Principle. Atomic number Z counts protons; mass number A counts protons plus neutrons. An ion changes electron count, not proton count. Isotopes differ in neutrons.

Decision. For a cation of charge +q, electrons = Z − q; for an anion of charge −q, electrons = Z + q.

Worked case. ²⁷Al³⁺ has 13 protons, 14 neutrons, and 10 electrons.

Remember. Periodic-table atomic mass is an isotope-weighted average, not a mass number.

lessons.title: Read a chemical formula
lessons.html:
Read a chemical formula

Principle. Subscripts count atoms in one formula unit; coefficients count whole formula units or moles. Ionic formulas must have zero net charge.

Decision. Balance ion charges before reducing subscripts; name transition-metal charge when variable.

Worked case. Al³⁺ and O²⁻ form Al₂O₃.

Remember. Never alter a subscript to balance a reaction.

lessons.title: Move among mass, moles, and particles
lessons.html:
Move among mass, moles, and particles

Principle. Molar mass converts grams to moles; Avogadro's constant converts moles to entities. The identity of the entity must be stated.

Decision. Use moles as the hub between different chemicals.

Worked case. 18.0 g H₂O ÷ 18.015 g mol⁻¹ ≈ 0.999 mol H₂O.

Remember. One mole of O₂ molecules contains two moles of O atoms.

lessons.title: Find an empirical formula
lessons.html:
Find an empirical formula

Principle. Turn each element's mass or percentage into moles, divide by the smallest mole amount, then multiply to clear near-integer fractions. Molecular formula is an integer multiple.

Decision. Check the final ratio against measured molar mass.

Worked case. 40.0% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O gives CH₂O; a molar mass near 180 g mol⁻¹ gives C₆H₁₂O₆.

Remember. Do not divide percentages directly without first converting to moles.

lessons.title: Balance, then convert
lessons.html:
Balance, then convert

Principle. A balanced equation conserves each atom and total charge. Coefficients supply mole ratios; mass ratios come only after molar-mass conversion.

Decision. Convert given mass → moles → coefficient ratio → desired unit.

Worked case. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: 3 mol O₂ could form 6 mol H₂O with enough H₂.

Remember. A coefficient never means a gram ratio.

lessons.title: Find the limiting reactant
lessons.html:
Find the limiting reactant

Principle. Calculate the product possible from each reactant separately; the smaller product amount is the theoretical yield. Actual yield divided by theoretical yield gives percent yield.

Decision. Compare product moles, not raw reactant masses.

Worked case. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: 2 mol N₂ and 3 mol H₂ give at most 2 mol NH₃; H₂ limits.

Remember. Excess reagent can remain even when the reaction stops.

lessons.title: Use molarity and dilution
lessons.html:
Use molarity and dilution

Principle. Molarity is solute moles per liter of solution. Dilution changes volume and concentration while conserving solute moles if no reaction occurs.

Decision. Use C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ only for dilution of the same solute.

Worked case. 25.0 mL of 2.00 M stock diluted to 100.0 mL becomes 0.500 M.

Remember. Solution volume is not necessarily solvent volume.

lessons.title: Write a net ionic equation
lessons.html:
Write a net ionic equation

Principle. Separate strong aqueous electrolytes into ions, preserve solids, liquids, gases, and weak electrolytes, then cancel unchanged spectator ions.

Decision. First predict whether a precipitate, gas, or weak electrolyte forms.

Worked case. Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).

Remember. Do not split a solid product into ions.

lessons.title: Track acid, base, and redox
lessons.html:
Track acid, base, and redox

Principle. A Brønsted acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts H⁺. Oxidation loses electrons; reduction gains electrons. Oxidation numbers expose the electron transfer.

Decision. Separate electron transfer from proton transfer before selecting a method.

Worked case. Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu: Zn oxidizes; Cu²⁺ reduces.

Remember. The oxidizing agent itself is reduced.

lessons.title: Link light to electronic change
lessons.html:
Link light to electronic change

Principle. Photon energy rises with frequency and falls with wavelength. Atomic line spectra arise from discrete electronic energy changes.

Decision. Use wavelength in meters and check whether emission or absorption occurs.

Worked case. A shorter-wavelength photon has greater energy.

Remember. Electron orbitals are probability distributions, not little planetary paths.

lessons.title: Build an electron configuration
lessons.html:
Build an electron configuration

Principle. Fill lower-energy orbitals first, obey two electrons per orbital with opposite spins, and place single electrons across equal-energy orbitals before pairing.

Decision. For transition-metal cations, remove electrons from the highest principal shell first.

Worked case. Fe: [Ar] 4s²3d⁶; Fe²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁶.

Remember. A configuration predicts valence behavior; it is not a drawing of fixed electron locations.

lessons.title: Predict periodic trends
lessons.html:
Predict periodic trends

Principle. Across a period, effective nuclear attraction generally grows: atomic radius falls while first ionization energy generally rises. Down a group, added shells enlarge atoms.

Decision. Account for subshell and electron-pair exceptions rather than treating trends as exact laws.

Worked case. Na is larger than Cl; Cl attracts a bonding electron pair more strongly.

Remember. Ionic size must be compared at a specified charge and electron count.

lessons.title: Draw Lewis structures
lessons.html:
Draw Lewis structures

Principle. Count valence electrons (adjust for ion charge), connect atoms, complete outer octets, then form multiple bonds when needed. Minimize unreasonable formal charges.

Decision. For each atom, formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − half the bonding electrons.

Worked case. CO₂ has O=C=O and zero formal charges.

Remember. Resonance represents a delocalized structure, not atoms rapidly switching bonds.

lessons.title: Use electron regions to find shape
lessons.html:
Use electron regions to find shape

Principle. VSEPR first counts bonding regions and lone pairs around the central atom. Electron-region geometry includes both; molecular shape names positions of atoms only.

Decision. A double bond counts as one region; lone pairs often compress bond angles.

Worked case. CH₄: tetrahedral; NH₃: trigonal pyramidal; H₂O: bent.

Remember. Polar bonds can cancel in a symmetric molecule such as CO₂.

lessons.title: Keep energy signs straight
lessons.html:
Keep energy signs straight

Principle. For the system, heat absorbed is positive and heat released is negative. At constant pressure, reaction heat equals enthalpy change. Reverse a reaction to reverse ΔH.

Decision. Use a Hess-law sum only after every equation has been transformed to the desired net equation.

Worked case. If combustion releases 286 kJ per mole of product, ΔH = −286 kJ mol⁻¹.

Remember. A favorable enthalpy change alone does not establish reaction speed.

lessons.title: Solve calorimetry
lessons.html:
Solve calorimetry

Principle. The temperature change is final minus initial. For ideal insulation, heat lost by one part is gained by the other. Use mass of the heated material with its specific heat.

Decision. Check whether the calorimeter itself absorbs heat.

Worked case. 100 g water warmed 5.0 °C absorbs about 2.09 kJ using c = 4.184 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.

Remember. Heat and temperature are different quantities.

lessons.title: Connect gas variables
lessons.html:
Connect gas variables

Principle. Ideal gas behavior relates pressure, volume, moles, and absolute temperature. At fixed T and n, P is inverse to V; at fixed P and n, V follows T.

Decision. Convert °C to K and use a gas constant consistent with pressure and volume units.

Worked case. At 1.00 atm and 298 K, 1.00 mol ideal gas occupies about 24.5 L.

Remember. At high pressure or low temperature, intermolecular forces and finite particle size matter.

lessons.title: Read a phase diagram
lessons.html:
Read a phase diagram

Principle. Each region marks the stable phase at that pressure and temperature. A boundary marks coexistence; the triple point joins three boundaries; the critical point ends the liquid–gas boundary.

Decision. Trace the actual P–T path before naming a phase change.

Worked case. Heating at pressure below the triple point can cause solid → gas directly.

Remember. For water, the solid–liquid boundary has an unusual negative slope.

lessons.title: Connect forces to properties
lessons.html:
Connect forces to properties

Principle. Dispersion exists for all particles; dipole interactions require permanent molecular dipoles; hydrogen bonding needs H attached to N, O, or F and a suitable acceptor.

Decision. For comparable size and shape, stronger attractions usually raise boiling point and lower vapor pressure.

Worked case. Water hydrogen bonds; methane has only dispersion forces.

Remember. A polar bond does not automatically make an entire molecule polar.

lessons.title: Separate rate from extent
lessons.html:
Separate rate from extent

Principle. A rate describes how quickly concentration changes; an equilibrium constant describes composition at equilibrium. A catalyst lowers the activation barrier in both directions but does not change K.

Decision. Use a rate law only when experimentally established; do not copy exponents from an overall equation.

Worked case. If rate doubles when [A] doubles with other conditions fixed, the observed order in A is one.

Remember. Fast does not mean product-favored.

lessons.title: Use reaction quotient Q
lessons.html:
Use reaction quotient Q

Principle. Write the equilibrium expression from activities, often approximated by concentrations for dilute solutions; omit pure solids and liquids. Compare present Q with K.

Decision. Q < K drives forward; Q > K drives reverse; Q = K is equilibrium.

Worked case. For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, Kc = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³).

Remember. Changing concentration changes Q immediately, not K at fixed temperature.

lessons.title: Set up an ICE calculation
lessons.html:
Set up an ICE calculation

Principle. Write initial concentrations, coefficient-scaled changes, and equilibrium concentrations. Solve the resulting equation and reject roots that give negative concentrations.

Decision. Test any small-x approximation against the final value.

Worked case. A ⇌ B starting with 0.10 M A: equilibrium A = 0.10 − x, B = x.

Remember. Do not add a solid's concentration to K.

lessons.title: Predict a shift
lessons.html:
Predict a shift

Principle. A concentration or pressure disturbance changes Q; the system evolves until Q returns to K. Only a temperature change changes K.

Decision. For gas pressure effects, compare gaseous mole counts on both sides.

Worked case. Compressing N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ favors the side with fewer gas moles.

Remember. A catalyst changes arrival time, not equilibrium position.

lessons.title: Translate pH
lessons.html:
Translate pH

Principle. pH and pOH are negative base-10 logarithms of hydronium and hydroxide concentrations. At 25 °C, their sum is 14.00.

Decision. Use concentration units mol L⁻¹, and know that 14.00 is temperature dependent.

Worked case. [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M gives pH 3.00.

Remember. A one-unit pH change is a tenfold concentration change.

lessons.title: Solve a weak-acid equilibrium
lessons.html:
Solve a weak-acid equilibrium

Principle. For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, Ka measures ionization. With initial HA concentration C and small ionization, [H⁺] ≈ √(KaC); verify x is small relative to C.

Decision. If the approximation fails, solve the full quadratic.

Worked case. Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, C = 0.100 M gives pH ≈ 2.87.

Remember. A weak acid need not have a high pH if it is concentrated.

lessons.title: Recognize a buffer
lessons.html:
Recognize a buffer

Principle. A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base in appreciable amounts. The ratio sets pH; total concentration sets how much added acid or base it can withstand.

Decision. Use Henderson–Hasselbalch only when both partners remain after reaction stoichiometry.

Worked case. Equal HA and A⁻ concentrations give pH = pKa.

Remember. At equivalence in a weak-acid/strong-base titration, the buffer pair is gone.

lessons.title: Read a titration curve
lessons.html:
Read a titration curve

Principle. Before equivalence, account for remaining acid/base and formed conjugate; at equivalence, identify the salt's hydrolysis; after equivalence, excess titrant dominates.

Decision. Half-equivalence for a weak acid gives pH = pKa.

Worked case. A weak-acid/strong-base titration has equivalence pH above 7 at 25 °C.

Remember. The steepest point locates equivalence, not necessarily pH 7.

lessons.title: Test precipitation
lessons.html:
Test precipitation

Principle. Ksp is the equilibrium product of dissolved ion activities raised to stoichiometric powers. Compare the current ion product Qsp with Ksp.

Decision. Qsp > Ksp implies precipitation is favored until equilibrium is reached.

Worked case. For AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻].

Remember. Common-ion addition generally lowers the salt's molar solubility.

lessons.title: Connect ΔG to equilibrium
lessons.html:
Connect ΔG to equilibrium

Principle. At fixed temperature and pressure, negative ΔG favors forward progress. Standard ΔG° reflects the standard state; actual ΔG depends on composition through Q.

Decision. At equilibrium ΔG = 0 and Q = K; a negative ΔG° implies K > 1.

Worked case. ΔG° = −RT ln K.

Remember. A spontaneous reaction can be kinetically slow.

lessons.title: Construct a galvanic cell
lessons.html:
Construct a galvanic cell

Principle. Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Electrons travel externally from anode to cathode; ions migrate through the salt bridge to maintain charge balance.

Decision. Compute E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode using reduction potentials; never multiply a potential by stoichiometric coefficients.

Worked case. Cu|Cu²⁺ || Ag⁺|Ag has E° = 0.80 − 0.34 = 0.46 V.

Remember. A galvanic cell has positive Ecell for the spontaneous written reaction.

lessons.title: Understand electrolysis
lessons.html:
Understand electrolysis

Principle. An external power supply drives an otherwise nonspontaneous redox change. The electrode names still follow oxidation at anode and reduction at cathode.

Decision. Charge in coulombs divided by Faraday's constant gives moles of electrons.

Worked case. 2 F of charge can deposit 1 mol Cu from Cu²⁺ if current efficiency is 100%.

Remember. Electrode polarity differs between galvanic and electrolytic setups.
